posts.title: Through #digitalization, we can ensure that the next frontier of the #energy transition is not only clean - but is just, fair
posts.caption:
Through #digitalization, we can ensure that the next frontier of the #energy transition is not only clean -  but is just, fair and inclusive for everyone, everywhere. 
 
Digitalization is already reshaping energy systems; transforming how power is generated, distributed and delivered to the 666 million people who still lack electricity. By 2035, AI could help reduce emissions by up to 5.4 GtCO₂e annually (more than the current total emissions of India) by accelerating smarter, low-carbon solutions in energy, mobility and food systems that are already emerging around the world: 
 
🇰🇪 In Kenya, digital twins and geospatial mapping are already helping identify underserved areas in real-time; guiding last-mile electrification and boosting resilience in off-grid systems. 
 
🇮🇳 India is using AI to forecast energy demand and optimize power flows in rural microgrids; ensuring efficient delivery while minimizing losses and emissions. 
 
🇨🇴 In Colombia, digital cold chains powered by renewables are supporting remote health clinics and smallholder farmers, enabling vaccine access and food security in underserved regions. 
 
A just, sustainable future runs on digital energy solutions - grounded in local leadership, resilience and inclusion.  
 
Discover how the Global South is already at the forefront of the digital energy revolution in the latest Sustainable Energy Bulletin: 👉 https://lnkd.in/e7PmUFtw 
 
#EnergyForDevelopment #DigitalForDevelopment #SustainableAI #EnergyAccess

posts.title: Too often, we treat the energy transition as something to be managed cautiously - especially when it comes to the role of you
posts.caption:
Too often, we treat the energy transition as something to be managed cautiously - especially when it comes to the role of young people. 
 
But the reality in the Global South tells a different story. In 2024, clean energy investments in electricity outpaced fossil fuels 7 to 1. This is not incremental progress; it’s a paradigm shift - one that youth are already helping to shape. 
 
As we accelerate into a future of electric vehicles, AI-integrated energy systems and smarter grids, we must reimagine, not just replicate, the systems we’ve inherited:

🔹 AI isn’t a silver bullet - its promise must not distract from the 1.18 billion people still living in energy poverty.
 🔹 EVs are only transformative if the benefits are shared - especially with communities in Africa, which holds over 50% of the world’s cobalt and manganese, yet often sees little value-added return.
 🔹 Energy is already central to climate action - cities use 78% of global energy and produce over 60% of emissions. The question isn’t whether to negotiate about energy, but how to ensure all voices are at the table.

Every day we should be working towards a sustainable energy revolution that addresses the needs and asks of people themselves. Young people are not simply  participants in this transition: they are already the dreamers, doers, and disruptors driving it forward. 

🎙 You can listen to my full reflections via the YOUNGO  Energy Podcast, available across all platforms: 👉 https://lnkd.in/eddJX87f

Let’s leap forward: not cautiously, but courageously. 

#EnergyForDevelopment #AIandDevelopment #YouthInEnergy #SystemsThinking

posts.title: Many countries in the Global South are actively working to advance energy transitions - even in the context of tight fiscal c
posts.caption:
Many countries in the Global South are actively working to advance energy transitions - even in the context of tight fiscal constraints.  

In my latest illuminem  article, I unpack the conversation on debt and the energy transition; not as parallel issues, but as deeply interconnected challenges shaping development trajectories: 🔗📘  https://lnkd.in/euFEESVQ

Reallocating a portion of the $1 trillion in global fossil fuel subsidies could create the fiscal space needed to accelerate sustainable, inclusive energy systems where they are most needed. That is why we need a different model - one that: 

➡️ Redirects fossil fuel subsidies - freeing up public funds that can better serve people and planet. 

➡️ Unlocks blended and concessional finance - to channel more of the 85% of clean energy investment not yet reaching the Global South. 

➡️ Aligns debt relief with climate ambition - easing pressure for the 54 countries that spend +10% of government budgets on debt service. 

➡️ Invests in long-term resilience - so regions like Africa, needing $200B annually for clean energy, can tap into the resources that they need. 

Debt is no longer just a macroeconomic indicator; it is shaping what is possible in energy, in equity, and in development. 

Getting this right isn’t just urgent. It’s foundational. 

#EnergyForDevelopment #DebtAndDecarbonization #DevelopmentFinance

posts.title: By 2030, data centers alone could consume up to 3–5% of global electricity; placing immense pressure on power systems, water
posts.caption:
By 2030, data centers alone could consume up to 3–5% of global electricity; placing immense pressure on power systems, water resources, and infrastructure, especially in regions already managing constrained resources.
 
In response, countries across Africa, Asia and Latin America are advancing regional, scalable, climate-smart pathways that the rest of the world can learn from:
 
🌐 In the SIJORI Growth Triangle (Singapore–Johor–Riau), cross-border compute sharing is helping to bridge infrastructure gaps and unlock regional AI innovation efficiently and affordably.
 
🌐 In Kenya, a clear geothermal policy attracted development finance, enabling Microsoft and a UAE partner to build a geothermal-powered data center - a scalable model for clean, resilient AI infrastructure in East Africa.
 
🌐 In Cambodia, Myanmar, and Laos, countries are exploring regional compute models to tap into underused capacity - scaling AI access without overloading national grids or diverting limited budgets.
 
The Global South is not just participating in the AI transition; it’s actively shaping how AI is built, powered, and governed to reflect the realities of people and communities themselves. 
 
Find out how else the Global South is shaping the next wave of AI infrastructure in the Sustainable Energy Bulletin: 👉 https://lnkd.in/e7PmUFtw
 
#EnergyforDevelopment #SustainableAI #DataCenters #SouthSouthCooperation #AIforGood

posts.title: What if regional power pools became the engine of an equitable energy future? As development aid declines (projected to fall
posts.caption:
What if regional power pools became the engine of an equitable energy future? 
 
As development aid declines (projected to fall by up to 22% this year) the Global South is stepping up, not stepping back. 
  
South–South trade now exceeds 28% of global trade. Regional blocs are leading, not following. And across Africa, Asia, and Latin America, countries are forging energy transitions on their own terms; through regional cooperation and shared infrastructure. 
 
🌊 Laos exports 100MW of hydropower to Singapore via Thailand and Malaysia - anchoring Southeast Asia’s growing cross-border electricity market. 
 
⚡ Ethiopia supplies up to 2,000 MW of surplus power to Kenya through a high-voltage line - contributing to Kenya’s leap from 37% to 79% electrification in just 10 years. 
 
🔋 The DRC and Zambia’s Special Economic Zone will produce battery precursors at one-third the cost of similar plants in the U.S.—laying the foundation for clean-tech manufacturing in Africa. 
 
These aren’t isolated successes: they’re signals of a seismic shift. South-South cooperation isn’t just working, it’s shaping the future of global energy..
 
🔗 Find out how else regional cooperation is accelerating energy transitions across the Global South: 👉 https://lnkd.in/eWKQbMuC
 
Regional integration is emerging as one of the most effective levers for expanding access, lowering costs, and building resilient, renewable energy systems at scale. To meet SDG7 by 2030, we must center these models; grounded in proximity, value and South-South leadership. 
  
#EnergyForDevelopment #JustTransition #SouthSouthCooperation #RegionalIntegration

posts.title: What if the world’s smallest island nations became the world's leaders in AI-powered clean energy? 🏝️⚡️ Small Island Developi
posts.caption:
What if the world’s smallest island nations became the world's leaders in AI-powered clean energy? 🏝️⚡️ 
 
Small Island Developing States (SIDS) are redefining what it means to be energy-resilient, digital-first and development-driven. While facing some of the most acute climate and energy vulnerabilities, they are turning digitalization into a catalyst for just energy transitions. 
  
More than 60% of SIDS import over 90% of their fossil fuels, resulting in energy costs up to four times higher than those in continental regions. Despite these structural challenges, many SIDS are setting ambitious climate targets, including 100% renewable energy by 2030 and net-zero emissions by 2050 - a bold shift toward resilience, self-reliance, and economic transformation. 
  
Digital innovation is helping SIDS leapfrog traditional energy systems and transform access: 
 
🔋 Fiji, Palau, and Kiribati are pioneering smart energy management through the Smart Islands Project—boosting grid resilience and enabling remote, low-cost electrification. 
 
📊 Guyana is scaling digital connectivity with over 200 ICT hubs, empowering Indigenous communities with data access for local energy planning. 
 
📡 Kenya’s Energy Access Explorer is now being adapted to island contexts, using geospatial AI to guide investment and electrification strategies. 
 
By fusing digital intelligence with decentralized renewables, SIDS are unlocking new models of energy equity, resilience and sustainable development. With the right investments in open data, smart infrastructure, and local capacity, these “digital islands” can lead the way for the Global South.  
 
To see other success stores and find out how else SIDS are redefining development pathways, I  invite you to read this UNDP  Policy Paper: 👉 go.undp.org/34Q
 
#EnergyForDevelopment #DigitalForDevelopment #SIDS #CleanTechLeadership
#RisingUpForSIDS
Kanni Wignaraja Alliance of Small Island States (AOSIS)

posts.title: What if the path to 1.5°C runs through the innovation corridors of the Global South? As the impacts of climate change intensi
posts.caption:
What if the path to 1.5°C runs through the innovation corridors of the Global South? 
 
As the impacts of climate change intensify, countries face a dual challenge: scale renewable energy and build inclusive, resilient economies.

The Global South is advancing on both fronts; not through incremental reform, but through cooperation, innovation and local value creation.

Modeling from UNDP  Charged for Change report shows that, with the right policies and investment, energy transitions could unlock universal access, reduce poverty by 193 million people and add $48 trillion to global GDP - all while staying within a 1.5°C pathway.

This transformation is not theoretical. It is already underway driven by a new development logic anchored in cooperation, innovation, and local value creation:
  
⚡ Under @ISA ’s Solar Initiative, over 570 clean energy scholars are advancing South-South R&D.
 
⚡ Indonesia has scaled mineral partnerships to grow nickel exports from $2B to $30B in just three years through value addition. 
 
⚡ DRC and Zambia are building a special economic zone to cut cathode precursor costs by 65%, while creating jobs and infrastructure.

⚡ Kenya is hosting geothermal-powered data centers, linking clean energy to digital development.

These are not one-off successes. They reflect a broader shift - where energy systems are being reimagined as engines of inclusion, productivity, and resilience.
 
The Global South is not waiting. It is redefining the future of energy.
 
🔗 Find out how the Global South is engineering a just transition through cooperation and innovation: 👉 https://lnkd.in/eWKQbMuC
 
#EnergyForDevelopment #SustainableAI #DigitalForDevelopment #SouthSouthCooperation

posts.title: On this #InternationalYouthDay, we celebrate the young people driving the energy transition - not in the future, but right no
posts.caption:
On this #InternationalYouthDay, we celebrate the young people driving the energy transition - not in the future, but right now. 
 
With over a quarter of the world’s population under 30yrs, and nearly 90% living in the Global South, youth are already creating, innovating and delivering the solutions that will define our shared energy future. 

Globally, the green economy could create 8.4 million jobs for young people by 2030 - yet data shows that youth still face barriers in accessing these opportunities. Connecting skills training, innovation ecosystems and inclusive policies will be critical to unlock their full potential.

This year’s theme, Local Youth Actions for the SDGs and Beyond, reminds us that progress happens where global ambition meets community leadership. With over 65% of SDG targets linked to local governance, youth engagement is not a luxury; it’s essential.

When given the space to lead, young people bridge the worlds of technology, policy and sustainability - turning dialogue into design; ambition into implementation; and local innovation into global impact. Across the Global South, it is the young engineers, economists, policymakers and change-makers who are already connecting renewable energy to human development, making it affordable, inclusive and resilient. 
 
From building local energy community microgrids to shaping policy, designing AI-driven clean cooking solutions and mobilizing climate justice movements, young people are proving that the energy transition is not a distant promise; it’s a reality being forged in real time. Their digital fluency, fresh perspectives, and unwavering commitment to the sustainable energy transition are bridging the gap between innovation and implementation.  

On this #InternationalYouthDay, let’s commit to working together to expand opportunities for youth in the sustainable energy revolution, and recognize that the leadership we need for a just, inclusive energy future is already here - transforming local action into global change.

#EnergyForDevelopment #JustTransition #YouthLed #InternationalYouthDay

posts.title: What if integrating renewables wasn’t just about cutting carbon - but also saving lives? Every year, air pollution from energ
posts.caption:
What if integrating renewables wasn’t just about cutting carbon - but also saving lives? 
 
Every year, air pollution from energy systems causes 6.4 million premature deaths, with the greatest burden falling on women and children in low- and middle-income countries. Power generation, cooking, transport, and waste burning all contribute to a silent epidemic - with energy and related sectors together responsible for over 70% of global GHG emissions.  Yet digitally powered solutions are already helping make energy and transport systems more efficient; reducing both emissions and their health impacts: 👉 https://lnkd.in/eNH_Vefp
  
While 666 million people still live without electricity and 2.1 billion rely on polluting cooking fuels, the global energy-health crisis is also a moment of powerful opportunity. Across the Global South, countries are demonstrating that integrating renewables, powered by digital innovation, can simultaneously reduce emissions and deliver major health gains: 
 
🌱 Kenya is using geospatial tools like Energy Access Explorer to plan hybrid grid-extension and distributed renewables, improving rural access and air quality. 
 
🌱 India is optimizing microgrids with AI to better match demand with renewable supply - reducing fossil fuel use and energy waste. 
 
🌱 Trinidad and Tobago is pursuing wind energy and green hydrogen, shifting away from fossil-powered generation that fuels both pollution and illness. 
  
Digital technologies like IoT sensors, AI forecasting, and remote monitoring also help utilities manage grid stability and enhance energy efficiency – reducing energy use in buildings and transport by around 10–15% while accelerating a healthier energy transition in real time. 
 
This isn’t just energy action; it’s a pathway to cleaner air, stronger health systems and more resilient communities. 
 
#EnergyForDevelopment #AirQuality #DigitalForDevelopment #HealthAndEnergy

posts.title: Grateful for the opportunity to join colleagues at @UNDPChina country office to to discuss how our new UNDP Strategic Plan 20
posts.caption:
Grateful for the opportunity to join colleagues at @UNDPChina country office to to discuss how our new UNDP Strategic Plan 2026–2029 puts sustainable energy at the center of development; not just as an enabler, but as a strategic lever for shifting the development curve itself. 

China’s experience shows why this matters. With 47% of global wind & solar; 20M EVs (half the global fleet); and having already achieved its 2030 renewables target six years early, China is proving that transitions can be nationally transformative and globally catalytic. But ultimately, this is not only about megawatts; it is about people, communities and systems for shared prosperity. 

In our dialogue, I shared three priorities for deepening China’s leadership and expanding shared progress: 

🔹 South–South and triangular cooperation
With 25 regional projects totaling 12 GW of new capacity worth $5B under the Shanghai Cooperation Organization, and partnerships across Africa, Asia and the Pacific, China is extending its leadership. The next step is moving from projects to scalable solutions grounded in governance, safeguards and inclusion. 

🔹 Digital, data & AI for energy systems
With grid investment projected at $100B annually and data center demand set to nearly double to 945 TWh by 2030, China is pioneering AI forecasting, digital twins and open data. Embedding these innovations into just transition frameworks is essential to ensure they deliver inclusive benefits 

🔹 Energy as a lever for human development 
As set out in the new Strategic Plan, success will not be measured only in megawatts, but in human outcomes: schools and clinics with reliable power; farmers with modern tools; households with clean cooking; and communities with greater resilience to crisis. 

At UNDP  we are proud to work alongside China and global partners to connect innovation with governance, finance, and inclusion. A just energy transition is not only a national achievement – it's a shared global responsibility. The real challenge is not how fast we expand renewables, but how effectively we connect them to the people who need them most. 

#EnergyForDevelopment #EnergyTransition #JustTransition #China

posts.title: It was a real pleasure to meet with my friend Dr. Gloria Magombo, Permanent Secretary for Energy and Power Development in Zim
posts.caption:
It was a real pleasure to meet with my friend Dr. Gloria Magombo, Permanent Secretary for Energy and Power Development in Zimbabwe, to reflect on how Zimbabwe can accelerate its energy transition in ways that put people, resilience, and prosperity at the center.
 
Our discussion touched on three priorities that are vital to unlocking this transformation:
 
🇿🇼 Supporting Zimbabwe’s National Clean Cooking Strategy With nearly 62% of the population still without access to clean cooking, and rural access below 10%, the new National Clean Cooking Strategy is more than an energy plan. It is a health plan, a gender equality plan, and an environmental plan. UNDP stands ready to support its implementation with policy expertise, innovative finance and local delivery models.
 
🇿🇼 Mission 300 Zimbabwe’s ambitious compact under Mission 300, targeting 100% electricity access by 2030 and raising clean cooking access to 70%, is a milestone moment. Building on our Solar for Health and mini-grid initiatives, UNDP  is committed to helping ensure these targets translate into real, reliable services for households, clinics, schools and enterprises.
 
🇿🇼 South–South cooperation and financial instruments Closing Zimbabwe’s annual energy gap - which currently costs the country 6.1% of GDP - requires innovative finance and regional collaboration. Instruments like the Renewable Energy Fund show how blended finance and South–South learning can unlock scale and inclusion.
 
Zimbabwe’s journey shows that energy is not only a national priority, it is a shared responsibility. By linking ambition with action, and innovation with inclusion, we can ensure the transition delivers for those who need it most.
 
#EnergyForDevelopment #JustTransition #CleanCooking #Mission300 #SouthSouthCooperation #Zimbabwe

Financing the global energy transition is no longer about if, but about how - and above all, for whom.

posts.title: It was a pleasure to join colleagues and partners at the Council of Engineers for the Energy Transition to reflect on how sus
posts.caption:
It was a pleasure to join colleagues and partners at the Council of Engineers for the Energy Transition to reflect on how sustainable energy can be a true lever for human development.
 
At a time when cooperation is under strain, sustainable energy remains one of the most powerful levers for progress - creating jobs, powering schools and clinics, advancing gender equality, and building resilience. Because in the end, the energy transition is never only about megawatts; it is about people and communities. Yet with 666 million people still without electricity and 2.1 billion without clean cooking, we must rethink where and how we act. That is why three priorities stand out:
 
⚡️ Clean cooking at scale - 2.1 billion people still cook with polluting fuels. Scaling clean cooking is not just about energy access, it is about saving lives, empowering women, and protecting the planet.
 
⚡️ Development assessment for a just transition - A just transition means linking energy to jobs, health, education, and resilience, so every investment delivers tangible benefits for people and communities.
 
⚡️ Harnessing digitalization & AI - Smart technologies can unlock grid capacity and optimize systems, but their true value lies in ensuring the transition is faster and fairer.
 
At @UNDP, our new Strategic Plan 2026–2029 positions energy as a strategic lever for shifting the development curve. With sustainable energy projects across 131 countries, we are already proving that the transition can be faster, fairer, and more transformative for people’s lives.
 
The technologies exist. The financing can be mobilized. The real challenge, and our shared responsibility, is ensuring no one is left behind.
 
#EnergyForDevelopment #JustTransition #SustainableEnergy #CleanCooking #AIforDevelopment

posts.title: It was a real pleasure to deliver the keynote at the Capacity Building and Training Parallel Forum: Advancing Global Carbon N
posts.caption:
It was a real pleasure to deliver the keynote at the Capacity Building and Training Parallel Forum: Advancing Global Carbon Neutrality Goals through Capacity Building. 

The momentum is undeniable: in 2024, renewables accounted for 92.5% of all new power generation, global clean energy investment surpassed $2.1 trillion, (more than double fossil fuels), and the renewable energy sector now supports 16 million jobs worldwide — with the potential to reach 40 million by 2050.  

But to turn this momentum into lasting impact, we must close the gap in capacity - the systems, skills and institutions that transform ambition into action: 

1️⃣ Investing in institutions & people - Every dollar invested in governance and skills can unlock tenfold in climate and energy finance. From Zimbabwe’s lithium policy to India’s incentives creating nearly 1M jobs, capacity is what translates ambition into investment and livelihoods. 

2️⃣ Scaling South–South & regional cooperation - Cooperation multiplies results. The African Continental Free Trade Area could unlock $9B annually, while lithium alliances in Latin America and nickel policies in Asia show how shared standards and supply chains accelerate progress. 

3️⃣ Leveraging innovation responsibly - From AI making grids 30% more efficient to monitoring systems hundreds of times faster, innovation is reshaping our energy systems in real-time. But to close divides rather than widen them, it must remain inclusive, affordable and people-centered. 

Carbon neutrality is not only a technological challenge. It depends on institutions, skills, finance and cooperation — and embedding capacity building into every layer of the transition. The opportunities are immense, if we choose to seize them. 

#EnergyForDevelopment #CarbonNeutrality #CapacityBuilding #SouthSouthCooperation #Innovation

posts.title: "Financing is not an end in itself; the real measure is the development it delivers." This was at the heart of the dialogue t
posts.caption:
"Financing is not an end in itself; the real measure is the development it delivers." 

This was at the heart of the dialogue that I co-convened with GEIDCO(Global Energy Interconnection Development and Cooperation Organization)  on “Bridging the Gap  Financing a Just and Inclusive Energy Transition.” 

We meet at a moment of paradox. Global clean energy investment will reach $2.2 trillion this year, yet less than 15% flows to developing economies outside China, and Africa, with its vast renewable potential, receives only 2% of that total. The challenge is not if the transition will be financed, but how - and whether it will be just, inclusive, and development-maximizing. From our panel session, three priorities came through strongly: 

🌏 Closing the financing gap through Southern leadership
From Africa’s green industrialization agenda to Asia-Pacific’s blended finance models, countries are already pioneering ambitious national strategies. The task now is to scale and aggregate pipelines to attract capital at the level required. 

🌏 De-risking & financial innovation as drivers of scale  
Sovereign green bonds in Indonesia, sukuk in the Middle East, and guarantee facilities in Africa show how innovative instruments can unlock billions. The next step is replication and mainstreaming. 

🌏 Maximizing development impact through energy investments  
Solarizing clinics in Zimbabwe, electrifying schools in Fiji, and powering farms in Bangladesh show how people-centered finance delivers. The task now is to scale these models so development outcomes define success. 

Grateful to Khaled Sharbatly , @Wang Yao, Pradeep Kurukulasuriya  Kurukulasuriya, @Yan Jing, and @Cheng Lin for their insights, and to @Beate Trankmann for reminding us that speed without fairness risks leaving people behind. 

At @UNDP, we believe the energy transition will only succeed if it delivers for people first: lighting homes, powering schools and opening opportunities across the Global South.

#EnergyForDevelopment #JustTransition #SustainableFinance #EnergyTransition

posts.caption:
Delighted and an honor to deliver the keynote at the Opening Ceremony at the 2025 Global Energy Interconnection Conference in Beijing on behalf of UNDP - a gathering that comes at a pivotal moment for the global energy transition.

One message stood out clearly: clean energy is no longer tomorrow’s promise. It is today’s most powerful tool for jobs, growth and true energy security. In 2023, the sector employed 16 million people worldwide, with China alone accounting for 7.4 million - nearly half the global total. By 2030, clean energy and efficiency could generate 70 million new jobs, with each $1 million invested in renewables creating nearly three times more jobs than fossil fuels

The shift is already reshaping economies. In 2023, clean energy accounted for 10% of global GDP growth - rising to 20% in China and nearly one-third in the EU. The question now is not whether the transition is happening, but how fast we can scale it and how effectively we can ensure its benefits reach the people who need them most.

It was in this context that @UNDP and @GEIDCO announced a new MoU: a commitment to deepen collaboration on innovative finance, South–South cooperation and digital solutions that can accelerate a just and inclusive energy transition.

We stand at a moment of great possibility. Clean energy is not only about megawatts—it is about unlocking opportunities to create millions of new jobs and livelihoods. It is a driver of transformative change across our societies, reshaping how we live, produce, and connect. And with the power of digital tools, data, and AI, we can ensure energy security that is smarter, more resilient, and inclusive. Together, we can build an energy future that truly leaves no one behind.

#EnergyForDevelopment #JustTransition #SouthSouthCooperation #GEI2025

posts.title: “Powering Inclusive Growth from Potential to Prosperity: Opportunities and Trade-offs in Green Hydrogen” Grateful to @Yu Zhuo
posts.caption:
“Powering Inclusive Growth from Potential to Prosperity: Opportunities and Trade-offs in Green Hydrogen” 

Grateful to @Yu Zhuoping, Amir Lebdioui , @Zhu Yongsheng, @Wang Ju, and @Zhang Jinxuan, who joined me at our UNDP  and GEIDCO(Global Energy Interconnection Development and Cooperation Organization)  high-level dialogue to explore how Asia-Pacific can ensure hydrogen drives inclusive growth, not just exports. 

But will incurred green hydrogen truly deliver for development? By 2050, green hydrogen could supply 12–22% of global energy demand, with Asia-Pacific at the center. The market, worth USD 8 billion today, could grow nearly eightfold by 2030. To get there, challenges around water (9 liters per kg), land (30,000 hectares of solar per million tonnes), and costs ($4.5–12/kg) must be managed, while scaling low-carbon hydrogen beyond today’s 1% share. And here, three priorities emerged from our discussion.

1️⃣ Align with development priorities: Green hydrogen must expand energy access, cut costs, and create jobs. If treated only as an export, communities risk being left behind. 

2️⃣ Embed safeguards: Large-scale hydrogen needs land, water, and minerals. Strong governance is vital to prevent water stress, land conflict, and inequality. 

3️⃣ Lead through cooperation: Regional partnerships on standards, infrastructure, and finance can amplify Asia-Pacific’s voice and build local value chains and skills. 

We explore these opportunities and trade-offs in more depth in our latest policy paper - Navigating the Currents of Green Hydrogen: 🔗 https://lnkd.in/e7f_tvA9 

At @UNDP, we believe the real promise of green hydrogen lies not in the technology alone, but in the choices we make today to ensure it drives inclusive, sustainable development for all. 

#EnergyForDevelopment #GreenHydrogen #JustTransition #InclusiveGrowth

Policy must steer innovation toward human development - powering clinics, creating jobs and building resilience across the Global South. 

At UNDP  we believe the energy transition will only succeed if it is inclusive - creating jobs, powering clinics and schools, and building resilience across the Global South. The question is no longer if AI will shape energy, but how we choose to direct it.

posts.title: Green hydrogen has been hailed as the "fuel of the future", and since 2020 it has appeared in more than 60,000 media headline
posts.caption:
Green hydrogen has been hailed as the "fuel of the future", and since 2020 it has appeared in more than 60,000 media headlines, with 58 countries and regional blocs now having adopted hydrogen strategies - half of them in developing economies. The market, valued at USD 7.98 billion in 2024, could grow nearly eightfold by 2030.
 
But there are also central challenges yet to navigate. Land and water requirements are extremely demanding for reaching scale, and current costs remain high at USD 4.5–12 per kilogram, while dependence on critical minerals adds new risks. Without deliberate safeguards, the green hydrogen economy risks reinforcing historical extractive models, and exposing first mover nations to lost investments without the right guidance on technologies and pathways.
 
That’s why UNDP, together with the  TIDE Centre, University of Oxford, published 📄 Navigating the Currents of Green Hydrogen: Towards a Human Development-Centred Framework, which I had the chance to co-write with Dr. Amir Lebdioui  and Pavel Bilek,  🔗 https://lnkd.in/eEXrfn9t
 
The policy paper introduces a 3P Framework—People, Planet, Prosperity to ensure strategies deliver inclusive development:
🔹 People: Expand energy access, upskill the workforce, and support a just transition.
🔹 Planet: Safeguard land, water, biodiversity, and minerals through strong governance.
🔹 Prosperity: Integrate hydrogen into industrial policy, foster local value chains, and phase investments.
 
This report offers practical policy levers for countries to steer green hydrogen at the right speed, time, and direction. With transparent governance and context-specific strategies, it can become a driver of just transitions and shared prosperity.
 
#GreenHydrogen #EnergyTransition #JustTransition #UNDP #Oxford

posts.title: Mission 300 Development Partners Coordination Group: Aligning for Impact Africa stands at an inflection point. Nearly 600 mil
posts.caption:
Mission 300 Development Partners Coordination Group: Aligning for Impact

Africa stands at an inflection point. Nearly 600 million people still live without electricity, yet the tools to close this gap—renewables, innovative finance, and new delivery models—are scaling faster than ever. The challenge is no longer just ambition, but delivery at pace and scale.

At today’s inaugural meeting of the Mission 300 Development Partners Coordination Group (DPCG), convened by the The World Bank Group  and the African Development Bank Group, I shared four key priorities that are essential to make Mission 300 a reality:

⚡ Joint forces for technical assistance and policy alignment: Coordinated support must go hand in hand with clear methodologies for measuring results, ensuring that productive energy use and clean cooking are fully embedded in national strategies.

⚡ Financial innovation and policy de-risking: Unlocking private capital at scale requires building bankable pipelines and sharing risk. UNDP  working with United Nations Capital Development Fund (UNCDF)  is advancing solutions to crowd in investment through guarantee schemes and blended finance mechanisms. Through the Africa Minigrid Programme, UNDP is supporting governments to create new regulatory frameworks and conduct Derisking Renewable Energy Investment (DREI) analyses—a strategic complement to other initiatives such as AfDB’s Africa Mini-Grids Market Acceleration Programme (AMAP).

⚡ Compact Delivery and Monitoring Units (CDMUs): Turning commitments into impact requires strong local ownership. UNDP is supporting CDMUs in Congo, Ethiopia, Tanzania, and Mozambique through the Italy-supported Energy for Growth Initiative, helping accelerate delivery on the ground by identifying pipelines of bankable projects.

At @UNDP, our strength lies in country presence, convening power, and delivery capacity. By joining forces with partners, we can transform ambition into reality—accelerating Africa’s energy transition and ensuring no one is left behind.

#EnergyForDevelopment #Mission300 #AfricaEnergyTransition #UNGA80

Carbon-Free Energy: Keeping up momentum on corporate commitments

Corporate ambition for carbon-free energy is higher than ever. Over 40% of the world’s largest 2,000 companies have net-zero pledges, covering more than 90% of the global economy. The challenge is no longer ambition; but turning pledges into action that is inclusive, transformative and delivers real impact.

At today’s @SEforALL convening during New York Climate Week, I had the pleasure of opening the session with a keynote, where I highlighted three priorities to move corporate climate commitments from ambition to action:

1️⃣ Smarter integration of AI and clean energy: Globally, AI-enabled systems could reduce electricity demand by up to 10% by 2030. In India, smart meters are already cutting distribution losses by 20%, while Brazil is advancing clean power-shoring to relocate industries to renewable hubs and cut emissions by up to 40%.

2️⃣ Scaling clean energy investment in the Global South: Sovereign green bonds in Bolivia and Chile and corporate PPAs in India & Kenya are already showing what’s possible. Scaling these models across Africa and Asia could unlock tens of gigawatts of new renewable capacity.

3️⃣ Going beyond emissions reduction: Net-zero must deliver jobs, resilience and equity. From Paraguay’s e-bus fleets to Rwanda’s solar irrigation with electric cargo bikes - boosting crop yields by 25% - clean energy and e-mobility are already transforming communities.

At @UNDP, we believe net-zero will only succeed if it is also just. Corporate climate action must go beyond compliance checklists to strategies that build competitiveness, resilience, and equity.

#EnergyForDevelopment #CarbonFreeEnergy #ClimateAction #JustTransition

posts.title: Can AI help power a Just Energy Future? Today, we stand at a crossroads. ChatGPT now reaches over 400 million weekly users, y
posts.caption:
Can AI help power a Just Energy Future?

Today, we stand at a crossroads. ChatGPT now reaches over 400 million weekly users, yet 1.18 billion people still live without reliable energy access. This paradox highlights both the promise and the peril of AI: it can deepen divides, or it can help us build more efficient, resilient and equitable energy systems.

In this piece, co-written with my colleague Stefano Pistolese , we argue that a new paradigm, “planetary intelligence” is emerging. By learning from nature and managing systems holistically, AI has the potential to transform not just energy, but the interconnected challenges of water, land, biodiversity and culture. To seize this opportunity, we must act on three fronts:

1️⃣ Move from biomimicry to “machine ecology”: AI can shift from copying nature’s designs to managing energy like an ecosystem. Smart grids already cut losses by 20%, and predictive tools balance renewables in real time. At scale, this could cut emissions 10% by 2030 and expand access.

2️⃣ Scale ecosystem-level solutions: AI modeled on natural systems can manage trade-offs across water, land, and biodiversity, creating up to $1.3 trillion in value by 2030 while safeguarding planetary health.

3️⃣ Ground innovation in equity: Efforts like Masakhane’s 40 African language models show how planetary intelligence can reflect diverse cultures, widening who benefits from AI and ensuring inclusion in the energy transition.

The question is not if AI will reshape our energy future, but how - and whether it will do so in a way that serves all people, not just a few. With the right governance, AI can become a catalyst for just and sustainable development.

👉 To find out more about planetary intelligence, I invite you all to explore my latest collaborative @illuminem article: https://lnkd.in/eRQ6mSsB

#EnergyForDevelopment #PlanetaryIntelligence #SustainableAI #AIforGood #climateweeknyc illuminem

posts.title: “SDG7 is not just one goal among many. It is the gateway to the entire 2030 Agenda.” Together with distinguished colleagues –
posts.caption:
“SDG7 is not just one goal among many. It is the gateway to the entire 2030 Agenda.”

Together with distinguished colleagues – @Annika Blakstad Otterstedt, Rana Ghoneim , @Daniel Schroth, and @Fanny Missfeldt-Ringius – I had the privilege to moderate the session “Mobilizing a Final Push on SDG7 and Roadmap towards the 2026 HLPF Review.”

We met at a moment of paradox. Energy poverty is the single greatest constraint on development, yet 9 out of 10 dollars in clean energy still go to advanced economies and China. Meanwhile, 666 million people remain without electricity and 2.1 billion without clean cooking. This is not simply a financial imbalance, it is a developmental divide.

But it is also a moment of opportunity. Renewables, innovative finance, and new delivery models are scaling faster than ever – and the conversation is now evolving from compacts to implementation. Through initiatives like Mission 300, partners are joining forces to move from commitments to concrete action, accelerating delivery on the ground and ensuring energy access translates into better health, learning and opportunity

From our discussion, three imperatives came through strongly:

🙏 Reinvent cooperation With ODA falling by over 9% in 2024 and projected to decline further in 2025, traditional aid cannot close the gap. New coalitions and partnerships are needed to reach those left furthest behind.

⚡ Build resilient value chains Solar modules now cost just $0.10 per watt, but tariffs and fragmented supply chains risk eroding gains. Demand for lithium has quadrupled since 2015, yet Africa and Latin America still lack processing capacity - exporting resources while importing expensive technologies.

🌐 Leverage AI for inclusion Electricity demand from data centers and AI grew 20% in just two years, and could match the consumption of Canada and the UK by 2030. But AI can also optimize grids, cut losses of 20-25% in some countries, and unlock efficiency for universal access.

At @UNDP, we believe the energy transition must be measured not just in megawatts, but in lives transformed. 

#SDG7 #EnergyForDevelopment #JustTransition #SustainableFinance #HLPF2026 #climateweeknyc

posts.title: Clean Cooking: From overlooked issue to global priority At today’s @UnitedNationsEnergy session on clean cooking, I was delig
posts.caption:
Clean Cooking: From overlooked issue to global priority

At today’s @UnitedNationsEnergy session on clean cooking, I was delighted to share why the clean cooking imperative must move from the margins of energy discussions to the center of sustainable development.

Every year, household air pollution from dirty cooking fuels causes 6.67 million deaths - more than malaria, tuberculosis and HIV/AIDS combined. The economic costs exceed $2.4 trillion annually, yet clean cooking receives < 1% of global energy investment, far below the $8 billion needed each year to reach universal access by 2030. We’re paying trillions to avoid spending billions.

To reframe this we must:

1️⃣ Integrate clean cooking into electrification planning – as is already happening in Zambia, where e-cooking is part of mini-grid expansion strategies, making entire systems more viable while supporting productive uses like food processing and irrigation.

2️⃣ Unlock innovative finance and market development – as is already happening in Tanzania, where the UNCDF-backed CookFund uses concessional loans and results-based finance to reduce end-user costs by up to 60%, proving that public capital can de-risk private investment and build viable markets.

3️⃣ Harness #digitalization, #AI, and IoT for innovation – as we are already seeing in Kenya, where IoT-enabled smart meters power pay-as-you-go LPG, letting households purchase fuel in $0.50 increments via mobile money, ensuring resilience even during COVID-19 lockdowns.

Momentum is building. The solutions are here. What’s missing is bold finance, political will and collective resolve.

#EnergyForDevelopment #CleanCooking #Health #SDG7 #climateweeknyc #unga80

posts.title: Africa holds 60% of the world’s best solar potential, a $190B clean energy opportunity. At yesterday’s fireside chat on #Afri
posts.caption:
Africa holds 60% of the world’s best solar potential, a $190B clean energy opportunity.
 
At yesterday’s fireside chat on #Africa’s energy future, I argued that innovation here must mean access and industrialization first—not just decarbonization. Momentum is real, but what’s missing is bold finance, regional integration, and political will to make Africa not just a consumer, but a clean energy engine.
 
The paradox is clear: with 60% of solar potential and 30% of critical minerals, Africa still has 600M people without electricity—85% of the global deficit—while receiving just 2% of clean energy investment. Without action, we risk a green-tech divide.
 
Countries in Africa are closing the gap by: 
1️⃣ Deploying decentralized innovation at scale – as is already happening in Kenya’s EcoSafi stoves which halve cooking costs; and Nigeria’s containerized mini-grids which  power villages in a day. Together, such models could reach 380M people by 2030 at the lowest cost.
2️⃣ Leveraging #digital and #AI breakthroughs – from UNDP  & IBM ’s geospatial forecasting tool to M-KOPA’s AI-driven financing, digital innovation is the backbone of Africa’s industrial revolution.
3️⃣ Turning mineral wealth into local prosperity – instead of exporting bauxite at $65/ton and importing aluminum at $2,335/ton, Africa must process locally. With copper, cobalt, nickel, and lithium worth $16T over 25 years, Sub-Saharan Africa could capture $2T by building domestic industries.
 
The opportunity is historic: with $190B/year in clean energy investment by 2030, Africa can close its access gap, fuel industrialization, and drive global energy innovation.
 
#EnergyForDevelopment #AfricaEnergyTransition #ClimateWeekNYC #Digitalization #SDG7

posts.title: Yesterday at a #UNGA80 side event on Data, Digital Transformation and the Resilience in the Energy Transition, I discussed a
posts.caption:
Yesterday at a #UNGA80 side event on Data, Digital Transformation and the Resilience in the Energy Transition, I discussed a defining question for the AI era:
 
AI is already reshaping the #energy transition - but does it build resilience, or deepen fragility?
 
Last year, in Mexico’s drought-stricken Querétaro region, farmers rationed water and lost crops. Just a few kilometers away, billions were invested in new AI data centers requiring extensive water cooling systems. The paradox is striking.
 
By 2027, data centers are projected to consume nearly 900 TWh of electricity and 6.6 billion cubic meters of water annually, largely driven by AI. But at the same time, AI also holds promise: it can optimize renewable grids, enable faster climate forecasting, and unlock billions in private finance for clean energy in the Global South.
 
During the discussion, youth delegates asked powerful questions:
👉 Are we using #AI in a way that advances sustainable energy for all?
👉 How can we prevent AI from becoming another burden on already stressed systems, and instead ensure it can create real opportunities for development?
👉 Will we step up to govern our energy transitions, so they are not only resilient, but also just?
 
The answers will define whether AI accelerates the clean energy future - or becomes another burden on already fragile systems.
 
#UNGA #AI #EnergyTransition #Resilience #Sustainability

posts.title: Planetary intelligence is the capacity for AI to steer global energy systems within ecological limits, integrating renewables
posts.caption:
Planetary intelligence is the capacity for AI to steer global energy systems within ecological limits, integrating renewables, storage, critical-mineral supply chains, and demand management so that innovation drives resilience and inclusive access.
 
This paradigm calls for digital systems that are distributed, operate within real-world resource constraints, and anticipate long-term impacts on energy security and equity. AI must strengthen the foundations of a just, reliable, and affordable energy transition - rather than increase fragility.
 
Already, AI data centers consume more electricity than 150 individual countries and could demand 6.6 billion m³ of water annually by 2027. The minerals powering this growth - lithium, cobalt, rare earths - are extracted largely from the Global South while most of the value accrues elsewhere. Unless guided by principles aligned with the concept of planetary intelligence, the Energy-AI nexus risks deepening these inequities.
 
The question is no longer whether AI will shape the energy transition - it already is. The real question is how to steer it so that the benefits, resources, and risks are shared fairly.
 
Read more in here in this blog I co-authored with Stefano Pistolese 👉 https://lnkd.in/eNzYmY7U
 
#JustEnergyTransition #AI #PlanetaryIntelligence

posts.caption:
Years of accelerating investments in renewables energy systems are paying off. Solar is now 41% cheaper than fossil fuels, and nearly 100 new climate commitments were announced last week at #UNGA80. 🔗 Read more in the new Sustainable Energy Bulletin: The Era of Energy Security 👉 https://lnkd.in/exUQY3mf 
 
This priority of energy security was highlighted during a high-level dialogue during UNGA80 on Ukraine’s energy recovery which underlined that solidifying a green and decentralized energy system is an imperative for national security. Similarly, public and private actors reaffirmed their commitment to Mission 300 for accelerating energy access that is not only accessible but also affordable and reliable.
 
But the finance bottleneck for resilience persists: countries and companies have pledged $1.6 trillion by 2030 under Energy Compacts, yet less than 0.1% of global climate finance goes to adaptation in energy systems. We must make resilience bankable - turning protection of people and infrastructure into an investment case at scale. The future of energy security will also hinge on innovation and optimization - exactly where the triptych of digital, data, and AI is central. AI-driven risk modeling, paired with robust analytics and digital platforms, can help investors and policymakers optimize targeted financing where it is most effective.
 
As we head toward #COP30 in Brazil, progress will be measured not only by how quickly we transition to renewables but by how resilient and inclusive those systems are.

posts.title: We often discuss the role of #AI in energy through percentage gains - efficiency improvements, cost reductions, predictive ac
posts.caption:
We often discuss the role of #AI in energy through percentage gains - efficiency improvements, cost reductions, predictive accuracy. But the real impact is structural: AI is enabling new market dynamics that redefine how energy systems are governed and financed.
 
The foundation is the data infrastructure: smart meters, sensors, and digital grids generate continuous insight into how electricity is actually used. This demand-side visibility creates a national load profile that can enable transformative opportunities,
 
Once governments can see real demand and private sector can act on this #data, new dynamics  emerge:
	•	Auctions can be designed around measured needs, defining clearer requirements for renewables, storage, and flexibility
	•	Investors can leverage data to lower risk and improve project bankability
	•	Markets gain credibility as public data limits discretion and reduces risk of corruption
But the same visibility that empowers can also expose vulnerabilities. Without strong governance, data monopolies, surveillance risks, and algorithmic bias could distort markets rather than open them.

posts.title: What if the future of AI wasn’t measured only in breakthroughs, but also in its true environmental cost? Global data centers
posts.caption:
What if the future of AI wasn’t measured only in breakthroughs, but also in its true environmental cost?
 
Global data centers consume about 460 TWh of electricity annually - around 1.5 % of global demand. The portion of this demand from AI is growing rapidly and could reach 85–130 TWh by 2030. If this trajectory continues, AI could emit up to 1.6 Gt CO₂e by 2035 even as its deployment in energy, food, and mobility offers potential avoidance of 3.2–5.4 Gt CO₂e annually.
 
Because #AI operates on land, water, and kilowatt-hours, its footprint is real, and growing. Unchecked growth risks worsening energy inequities: many regions already grapple with power shortages, yet AI infrastructure is concentrated in the Global North.
 
By redesigning AI to align with planetary boundaries, we can mitigate its impact:
⚡ Transition data centers to 100 % renewable energy with transparent sourcing.
💧 Innovate in cooling systems to minimize water use and recycle heat for communities
📊 Promote efficiency standards and “green AI” benchmarks to guide responsible innovation
🌐 Ensure equitable access so the Global South benefits from AI advances, not just bears the costs
 
At the same time we can leverage its system benefits:
+⚡ AI optimization has already improved renewable-grid efficiency, raising wind power’s market value by up to ~20 %.
+💧 AI-based forecasting now prevents climate damages worth up to $50 billion annually through early-warning systems.
+📊 Optimization in logistics and manufacturing has already saved over 3 million metric tons of packaging material since 2015.
+🌐 Expanding sustainable AI infrastructure can accelerate investment in low-carbon technologies, projected to require $2.4 trillion annually by 2030 in emerging economies. 
 
To explore this further, I invite you to read my latest collaborative illuminem  article with my colleague Stefano Pistolese : 👉 https://lnkd.in/eRQ6mSsB 
 
#EnergyForDevelopment #JustTransition #DigitalForDevelopment #AIforGood

For decades, we’ve built energy grids around industry. But what if we did the opposite, and built industry and data centers around renewable energy sources?
 
This is the idea at the center of “powershoring”, which takes the approach of placing energy at the center of development literally, turning energy geography into economic strategy.
 
🇧🇷 Brazil is already positioned to apply this strategy. After years of expanding generation capacity faster than demand, Brazil holds an electricity surplus - a rare challenge in a world of energy scarcity. Under an agenda of green neoindustrialization, regions rich in wind power are attracting new investment in energy-intensive manufacturing, linking industrial growth directly to clean energy.
 
Learn how countries are turning their just energy transitions into a foundation for industrial growth in our latest Sustainable Energy Bulletin 👉 https://lnkd.in/eBAMvFDe

posts.title: Over half of the beneficiaries of UNDP's energy portfolio are in countries in crisis settings. So what have we learned? 🔸Firs
posts.caption:
Over half of the beneficiaries of UNDP's energy portfolio are in countries in crisis settings. So what have we learned?
 
🔸First, that digital tools are changing how we can scale resilient energy systems. Geospatial mapping, digital twins, and AI-based risk models are transforming how we can mitigate vulnerability.
 
🔹Second, that energy is foundational infrastructure for recovery. An investment in energy infrastructure is an investment in rebuilding water services, health, communications, and livelihoods.
 
♦️Third, that in fragile contexts, energy finance is beyond risk mitigation; it’s about making resilience bankable. Less than 0.5% of global adaptation finance reaches energy systems. Countries are leveraging mechanisms like parametric insurance and regional risk pools to bring multiples on returns in investment.
 
These efforts are already accelerating - from solarizing hospitals and clinics in Yemen, to restoring decentralized power in Ukraine, to bringing renewable energy to crisis-affected communities across Sudan, Somalia, and the Sahel. posts.title: “Energy resilience” is not a uniform concept - it reflects distinct structural realities across regions and context. 🔵 In man
posts.caption:
“Energy resilience” is not a uniform concept - it reflects distinct structural realities across regions and context.

🔵 In many crisis settings, it refers to continuity under disruption - distributed solar and storage systems keeping essential services operational amid physical and cyber risks.

🟠 In Central Asia, it implies interdependence - regional power pools projected to reduce generation costs by 8 percent through shared reserves and cross-border balancing.

🟢 In Sub-Saharan Africa, it denotes reliability - systems that can sustain demand growth and climate stress while extending access to those still excluded.

🔴 In Latin America and the Caribbean, it means protection - coastal grids redesigned with underground cabling and wind assets certified for category-five storms.

Yet, less than 1 percent of global adaptation finance is directed toward energy systems, despite investments in resilience returning multiples in gains in avoided losses and productivity.

Energy resilience binds infrastructure to governance, data to finance, and technology to social stability. In development terms, it is the capacity of an energy system to maintain function, equity, and trust when the environment around it changes.

Read more in the Sustainable Energy Bulletin - The Era of Energy Security 👉 https://lnkd.in/eBAMvFDe

#EnergyForDevelopment #EnergyResilience

posts.title: Across Africa, the energy revolution is accelerating. Investments in renewables have nearly tripled since 2019, and solar is
posts.caption:
Across Africa, the energy revolution is accelerating. Investments in renewables have nearly tripled since 2019, and solar is now the least-cost source of power in most African markets.

This transformation holds immense opportunity. Africa possesses around 60% of the world’s best solar resources, yet only 1% of installed solar capacity. Unlocking this potential could power homes and industries, create over 3 million new green jobs by 2030, and drive inclusive growth from the ground up. But for this revolution to deliver lasting development impact, it must be just - anchored in governance, innovation, and digital empowerment.

1️⃣ Strengthen Governance
Establish transparent, accountable institutions with continent-wide standards for procurement, land use, and revenue sharing to ensure renewable wealth translates into jobs, community benefits, and public trust.

2️⃣ Mobilize Innovative Finance
Move from isolated projects to bankable investment pipelines. Blended finance, risk guarantees, and local-currency mechanism can de-risk markets and crowd in private capital. By mobilizing the estimated $190 billion per year needed by 2030, African countries can power inclusive industrialization and deliver universal energy access.

3️⃣ Harness Digital, Data & AI
Leverage AI and digital tools to make systems smarter and more affordable. Predictive analytics can cut project costs by 15%, and generative AI - if locally embedded in value chains - could unlock over $100 billion in annual economic value.

Africa’s energy revolution is not a story of scarcity but one of sovereign opportunity. With the right governance, finance, and digital backbone, the continent can transform its renewable wealth into sustainable development and true energy independence.

#EnergyRevolution #JustEnergyTransition

posts.title: The energy transition is about more than climate - it is about sustainable jobs, sovereignty, and inclusive economic growth.
posts.caption:
The energy transition is about more than climate - it is about sustainable jobs, sovereignty, and inclusive economic growth. We need to refocus on human development at the center of energy.

Clean #energy now employs 35 million people worldwide, yet women represent only 32% of that workforce. Global investment has surpassed USD 2 trillion, outpacing fossil fuels—but translating this momentum into affordable, reliable, and inclusive energy remains the real challenge.

Smarter, decentralized systems can shift this balance. #Digital tools, #AI, and data-driven management can optimize demand, reduce losses, and improve reliability—helping every unit of energy power growth and resilience. Smarter grids alone could cut 1 gigaton of CO₂ annually and lower peak loads by 8–12% by 2050, while digitally enabled efficiency in public buildings can reduce energy use by up to 50%.

Yet energy and digital transitions are advancing faster than the systems that govern them and mitigate their risks. The priority now is pairing governance with institutional capacity and national innovation systems to make energy systems fairer, smarter, and more resilient.

This week in Skopje, I am pushing to advance these priorities during the 14th International Forum on Energy for Sustainable Development, focusing on scaling up action toward aligning innovation, governance, and human development for a just energy future.

#EnergyForDevelopment #DigitalTransition #UAEConsensus #IFESD

posts.title: Globally, renewable-power capacity is projected to increase by around 4,600 GW between 2025 and 2030. The opportunity now is
posts.caption:
Globally, renewable-power capacity is projected to increase by around 4,600 GW between 2025 and 2030. The opportunity now is to ensure our digital, data, and human systems can absorb this growth—by strengthening coordination, governance, and skills to drive the structural change required for a just energy transition.

Today during Day 2 of the 14th International Forum on #Energy for Sustainable Development in Skopje, I moderated a discussion centered on how digitalization, data, and AI can help overcome these limits—and the new vulnerabilities they create.

1️⃣ First, the main bottleneck for renewable adoption is now absorption capacity. Grids cannot integrate trillions of USD of investment in renewables without parallel investment in #digital coordination, data systems, and human expertise. If a solar panel lacks a sensor, it effectively doesn’t exist to the system.

2️⃣ Second, #AI must remain a decision-support system, not an autonomous agent. Human oversight and digital skills are essential—especially as clean-energy jobs now account for more than half of the world’s 67 million energy-sector jobs.

3️⃣ Third, a just energy transition requires algorithmic justice. Without inclusive data governance and intentional design, algorithms trained on developed grids will reinforce the very access gaps they could help close.

4️⃣ Fourth, flexibility remains the cheapest untapped resource. Yet, fragmented regulation still blocks dynamic tariffs and peer-to-peer trading. Digital tools can help realign incentives for consumers to use energy when renewables are abundant. Unreliable grids could otherwise cost developing economies $1.3 trillion in lost output by 2030.

Ultimately, the digital, #data, and AI revolution must serve human development. These tools are already creating new market dynamics that are redefining how energy systems are governed and financed, but we need to always be vigilant to preserve our focus on what actually matters: people.

#DigitalTransition #EnergyTransition #AIForEnergy #IFESD

posts.title: Today during the third day of the International Forum on #Energy for Sustainable Development in Skopje, I joined young leader
posts.caption:
Today during the third day of the International Forum on #Energy for Sustainable Development in Skopje, I joined young leaders for the “Youth in Energy” session to discuss their key role in shaping the revolution of energy, development, and digitalization — not as the generation of the future, but of the present. Some key actions that arose from the discussion included:

1️⃣ Invest in youth as the #digital natives of the energy transition
The world’s 1.8 billion young people are increasingly central as a creative power accelerating the energy revolution. In the Global South, entrepreneurs are three times more likely to start a business than peers in the Global North — yet over 90% of these ventures remain in informal markets. In Latin America, 36% of new entrepreneurs are under 34, but only 5% of youth-founded firms last beyond three years. Investing in reliable energy access, digital infrastructure, and early-stage finance can turn survival enterprises into scalable green innovators.

2️⃣ Build national innovation ecosystems that link ideas to markets
Youth have the creativity; what’s missing are the structures that connect their ideas to opportunity. Less than 1% of finance reaches youth-led solutions, and less than 1 in 8 young workers has formal training in green or digital skills. Governments must align education, finance, and entrepreneurship policies into national innovation ecosystems — frameworks of actors, institutions, and policies that generate, implement, and diffuse new technologies and knowledge.

3️⃣ Catalyze #youth entrepreneurship to become engines of jobs and inclusion
The task is not only to train youth but to enable them to create markets — through public procurement, incubators, and demand-driven programs. In Ghana, an agritech initiative is training 300,000 young people in AI, biotechnology, and green innovation to power modern value chains. Replicating such models can turn youth enterprises into digitally-enabled impact that can create inclusive jobs.

When young innovators can access finance and markets within larger innovation systems, they become true partners in accelerating the just energy transition.

#YouthInEnergy #JustEnergyTransition #EnergyForDevelopment #IFESD

posts.title: The energy transition is about acceleration, how quickly we can scale renewable integration. Digital, #data, and AI enable th
posts.caption:
The energy transition is about acceleration, how quickly we can scale renewable integration. Digital, #data, and AI enable that speed — but we must not trade quickness for justice.

In Skopje this week during the 14th International Forum on Energy for Sustainable Development, I questioned, how can we shift the conversation from digital optimization to digital integrity?

#AI can now forecast grid conditions in near real time, anticipate renewable variability, and optimize power flows across billions of data points. Predictive analytics alone could unlock 175 GW of transmission capacity and cut peak loads by 12% — proof that digital systems can make grids both efficient and smarter.

But the faster we move, the less time we leave to verify the quality, origin, and bias of the data itself. In 2024, 4,875 cyber incidents were recorded across the energy and critical-infrastructure sectors — a sharp reminder that every new sensor and data link can also be an entry point for risk. And as 83 percent of urban residents are online compared with just 48 percent of rural populations, the same connectivity gaps that divide access also shape the data that train AI models.

Without open, interoperable, and verifiable systems, we risk building a transition that is more efficient — but not more equitable.

The technologies exist. What’s missing is sustained political will and coordination to ensure that data, AI, and markets work for people, not just performance. The #energy transition will not be powered by technology alone — but by the integrity of the systems and data it rests on.

#DigitalTransition #AIforEnergy #EnergyGovernance IFESD – 14 / 14th International Forum on Energy for sustainable development _14

posts.caption:
🇬🇪 Georgia is harnessing renewable energy, digital systems, and cross-border connectivity to power new era of regional development.

During my discussion with Ms. Inga Pkhaladze , Deputy Minister of Economy and Sustainable Development of Georgia, we reflected on how Georgia is accelerating its energy transition with both speed and integrity.

Georgia is positioning itself as a renewable energy bridge to Europe. The Black Sea Submarine Cable, a ~1.3 GW high-voltage link between Georgia and Romania, will redefine regional energy trade, and Azerbaijan’s parallel plan for an additional 4 GW connection could transform the Black Sea into a new corridor of renewable exchange connecting the Caucasus, the EU, and Türkiye.

Beyond the grid, #Georgia’s ambitions stretch further — toward becoming a regional digital hub for #energy, expanding battery storage and recycling to build resilience, and oppportunities to explore green hydrogen for domestic use and export. Our discussion focused on the next phase: ensuring that new markets are cyber-secure, data-transparent, and ready for balancing, storage, and cross-border trade. 

Georgia is expanding off-grid solar solutions to bring electricity to remote communities, yet as solar panels arrive, the next challenge begins: ensuring local capacity to maintain them and to ensure they bring not only access but also build livelihood. harnessing data to identify data poverty and opportunities 

As the Deputy Minister put it, the question is not just how to generate more power — but how to generate more opportunity.

Douglas Webb Omar/Memo Tsereteli Ivana Zivkovic

posts.title: ⚡ Energy finance is about architecture — building systems that investors and citizens can both trust. In 2024, global renewab
posts.caption:
⚡ Energy finance is about architecture — building systems that investors and citizens can both trust. In 2024, global renewable investment reached USD 624 billion, yet less than 15 percent reached developing economies outside China — and only 2–3 percent to Africa. 

The task ahead is not just to mobilize more capital, but to unlocking opportunities for clean energy where the need and potential are greatest. That requires financial and institutional systems capable of structuring, verifying, and absorbing investments at scale.

At the 14th International Forum on #Energy for Sustainable Development in Skopje, leaders from across regions agreed: capital follows credibility. A few ways they converged on we can do this:

1️⃣ Build national financing ecosystems, not fragmented projects, that can enable bankability of projects.
Energy-efficiency funds in Kosovo, Jordan, and Moldova show these financial mechanisms. The key for bankability starts with structuring projects with clear revenue models, transparent governance, and measurable performance to minimize investor risk.

2️⃣ Aggregate small projects to match investor logic.
Commercial lenders seek diversification. Aggregating small clean-energy projects — solar rooftops, retrofits, micro-grids — into verified portfolios lowers risk premiums and opens new credit lines for municipalities and SMEs. Inclusion also remains the ultimate de-risking strategy, as funds led by women in risk-management roles have proven on average lower default rates.

3️⃣ Embed data integrity into all financial instruments as the foundation of credibility.
Accurate baselines, open performance data, and auditability are now prerequisites for green finance. In Africa, the @AFREC Energy Information System is helping lenders quantify risk and track national progress with greater confidence. Digital monitoring and AI-driven analytics can accelerate access to finance — but ensuring the datasets they are built on are equitable remains central.

The real measure of progress will be how fast we can turn global liquidity into local legitimacy — through institutions capable of absorbing, managing, and sustaining capital.

#EnergyFinance #JustEnergyTransition #FinanceForDevelopment #EnergyForDevelopment #IFESD_14

3️⃣ Industry must create dignity. With 360 million young Africans entering the workforce in the next decade, inclusion is not a social goal - it’s an economic imperative. When women and youth lead, productivity and innovation rise together.
 
If the first industrial revolution was powered by coal, Africa’s will be powered by cooperation; between nations, investors, innovators and communities. Let’s move from potential to progress, and from progress to prosperity that endures.🌐🙏

posts.title: Last week, I had the opportunity to sit down with RASHID ABDALLAH, Executive Director of the African Energy Commission of the
posts.caption:
Last week, I had the opportunity to sit down with RASHID ABDALLAH, Executive Director of the African Energy Commission of the African Union  (AFREC), to discuss how data is reshaping Africa’s energy transition.

Data availability goes beyond merely monitoring progress; it plays a crucial role in de-risking investments and assisting governments and development partners in targeting projects and programs where they are most needed.

However, over 40 percent of African countries still depend on outdated or incomplete electricity data, which limits their ability to design effective policies or attract financing.

Since 2012, the African #Energy Information System, led by AFREC, has been enhancing the collection, validation, and dissemination of national energy data across the continent. Through capacity-building for national focal points, harmonization of data standards, and partnerships with regional and international organizations, AFREC is steadily improving the quality, credibility, and comparability of Africa’s energy data landscape.

In my discussion with Rashid, we explored how this initiative can align with UNDP ’s efforts to utilize geospatial analytics to move beyond binary indicators of energy access, aiming to understand how, where, and how effectively energy is used. After all, what does “access” mean if the energy is neither affordable nor reliable?

What innovations do you see as most promising for improving energy data availability? How can we ensure that #data-driven energy strategies translate into affordability, reliability, and equity? 

#JustEnergyTransition #DataForDevelopment #UNDP #AFREC #EnergyData Ahunna Eziakonwa Damilola Ogunbiyi Francesco La Camera Marcos Neto

posts.title: 🌍 As COP30 opens in Belém this week, the call to triple renewable energy capacity and accelerate just energy transitions has
posts.caption:
🌍 As COP30 opens in Belém this week, the call to triple renewable energy capacity and accelerate just energy transitions has never been more urgent. AI and digital technologies are reshaping how energy is produced, traded, and managed. But as systems become more digitalized, the risks also increase, spanning data governance, algorithmic control, cybersecurity, and corruption in emerging value chains.

In 2024 alone, nearly 4,900 cyber incidents hit the energy and critical-infrastructure sectors. Addressing these risks is essential to ensuring that digital and AI-enabled energy systems expand equitable access rather than concentrate advantage. Today, we are pleased to share a new UNDP policy paper: 

 ⚡ Energy, Digital, and Anticorruption: Leveraging AI and Digital Innovation for Governance in the Just Energy Transition 👉 https://lnkd.in/eCM--xkt

It offers actionable pathways on how AI and digital innovation can power cleaner, fairer, and more accountable energy systems:

1️⃣ Boost public-sector capacity. Bridging the AI gap between regulators and companies is key to fair and accountable energy markets, especially as global investment in the energy transition is projected to reach $4 trillion annually by 2030.
2️⃣ Increase transparency in markets and supply chains. India is using digital tools to boost transparency, reduce energy losses that once exceeded USD 16 billion annually, and attract new investment in the power sector.
3️⃣ Enable smarter energy planning. Combining AI and blockchain is optimizing energy demand, production, and distribution. In the UAE, Dubai’s state-owned utility DEWA uses AI-driven smart grids to predict electricity demand and manage supply more efficiently.
4️⃣ Mitigate corruption in critical minerals and decentralized energy. With demand for minerals like lithium, nickel, and cobalt projected to surge by up to 900% over the coming decades, responsible digital governance is vital to curb corruption and ensure sustainable access.

This policy paper offers practical pathways and examples from Brazil, Estonia, India, Ukraine, and others to illustrate how digital innovation and integrity systems can support cleaner, fairer, and more accountable energy transitions across countries.

posts.title: Green #hydrogen is projected to be able to reach 7-8% of final energy demand by 2050, more than double the needs of the entir
posts.caption:
Green #hydrogen is projected to be able to reach 7-8% of final energy demand by 2050, more than double the needs of the entire shipping sector today.

But hydrogen must complement—never replace—development objectives.
 
At today’s #COP30 dialogue organized by the Council of Engineers for the Energy Transition  and Sustainable Energy for All (SEforALL) , I steered the discussion to explore how to ensure green hydrogen supports national development priorities, protects ecosystems, and creates shared prosperity.

1️⃣ Align hydrogen with national development priorities:
When tied to national strategies, these investments can decarbonize hard-to-abate sectors and build local industry and energy security. Without this, they risk becoming extractive, with value exported and impacts retained.

2️⃣ Strengthen governance across the land–water–energy system
Hydrogen is not a standalone investment—it depends on water resources, land availability, and grid capacity. In Namibia, a 2-million-tonne project would require 18 million m³ of water annually, equivalent to the needs of more than 250,000 people. Countries need integrated planning, clear regulation, and national innovation systems.

3️⃣ Ensure hydrogen creates local prosperity, not only export pathways:
Not every country can or should pursue large-scale hydrogen. The right pathway depends on water availability, land constraints, energy access needs, and industrial priorities.  Where hydrogen is viable, it must deliver domestic value: but in local jobs, resilient value chains, and equitable benefits.
