posts.title: At the Africa Investment Forum’s Mission 300 Day in Rabat for a new-era partnerships, stronger national delivery capacity, an
posts.caption:
At the Africa Investment Forum’s Mission 300 Day in Rabat for a new-era partnerships, stronger national delivery capacity, and smart financing architectures.

The success of Africa’s energy transformation will not be measured by kilometres of cable laid, but by households switching on lights, health centres powering lifesaving equipment, and businesses growing with reliable, affordable electricity. Africa’s infrastructure is expanding fast—yet millions of connected households remain in the dark. Not only because the grid never reached them, but because they cannot afford to use it. 220 million Africans cannot afford basic electricity consumption, and 400 million cannot afford 500 kWh/year, barely a tenth of an average European household.

This affordability gap is one of the defining challenges for Africa’s economic future—but also a real opportunity to shape a new energy paradigm: one where investments are targeted, financing costs fall, and partnerships drive scalable, country-led solutions.

At the Africa Investment Forum’s Mission 300 Day in Rabat, I reaffirmed UNDP’s commitment to universal electrification in line with the UN-Energy Pledge. I had the pleasure to reflect with Aboubacar Said Anli, Minister of Energy, Water, and Hydrocarbons, #Comoros, Nialé Kaba, Minister of Minister of Planning and Development, #Côte d’Ivoire, Michael Franz , Team Leader, GET. Invest and moderated by Daniel Schroth Director at African Development Bank Group  , on how to ensure electricity is not only available but affordable, inclusive, and transformative:

1️⃣ Shift from counting connections to measuring development outcomes — in health, education, livelihoods, and productivity.
2️⃣ Reduce the cost of capital, which is 3–4 times higher in Africa; narrowing this gap can cut project costs by 15–25%.
3️⃣ Strengthen partnerships across governments, DFIs, development partners, and the private sector to align financing and delivery at scale.

This is where Mission 300 becomes catalytic. With coordinated compacts, unified delivery frameworks, and blended investment pipelines, #M300 shows how strategic partnerships can amplify impact, accelerate financing, and translate ambition into real improvements in people’s lives. UNDP stands with the The World Bank , AfDB, and all Mission 300 partners in transforming energy systems into engines of development, inclusion, and resilience.
Kevin KARIUKI The Global Energy Alliance for People and Planet

posts.title: Energy took center stage during COP30 Brazil, but while the Belém Package moved negotiations forward, calls from 80+ countrie
posts.caption:
Energy took center stage during COP30 Brazil, but while the Belém Package moved negotiations forward, calls from 80+ countries to include phase-out language on fossil fuels didn’t make the final text. As SG Guterres warned — a 1.5°C overshoot is humanity’s red line.
 
Negotiations set the ambition, but implementation will define success. To meet UAE Consensus targets, the world needs 1,122 GW of new renewables every year from 2025 — a 16.6% annual growth rate — even as 90% of renewables were cheaper than fossil fuels in 2024. The challenge isn’t only speed, but who benefits and who carries the cost of this transition.
 
The Baku-to-Belém roadmap aims to scale climate finance to $1.3T annually by 2035, triple adaptation finance, and institutionalize a Just Transition Work Program. Yet efficiency gains remain slow with only 1% improvement in 2024.
 
This is where #digitalization and #AI can accelerate progress — if designed for people and planet. The new Technology Implementation Program, especially if linked to the idea of planetary intelligence, can offer a path to align clean energy, digital systems, and nature rather than trade between them.
 
Read more in The Energy Revolution: Beyond Humanity’s Red Line  👉 https://lnkd.in/eSZqrmks
 
#JustEnergyTransition #EnergyForDevelopment

posts.title: A just energy transition is not simply a technological shift. It is a development strategy. — it is social policy, industrial
posts.caption:
A just energy transition is not simply a technological shift. It is a development strategy. — it is social policy, industrial policy, climate policy, and a development priority all at once. 

This week, I’m with @UNDP colleagues in Dakar, Senegal, alongside 20+ country offices, energy experts, financiers and development practitioners to focus on what matters most: turning clean energy into development outcomes. 

Africa holds the world’s greatest renewable potential — including 60% of global high-quality solar and nearly 8,000 GW of solar capacity — and 30% of critical mineral reserves, positioning the continent to lead the green industrial economy.

How can we re-think Africa’s economic transformation through a just energy transition? 

Three opportunities will define its transition:
 
1️⃣ First, Africa is becoming central to the global clean-energy economy, building on green industry. Africa can go behind producing clean power — it can also industrialize it, from agro-processing to e-mobility to mineral value chains. A transformation that could save 3.7 million lives every year. 

2️⃣  Second, de-risking is essential to unlock finance at scale. Africa needs USD 190–200 billion annually for energy investment, yet risk is perceived at 2–3× reality. Blended finance, guarantees, and policy reform can flip this equation and turn pipelines into projects. 

3️⃣  Third, digitalization and AI make this transformation even more powerful, as scaling energy access is an economic imperative, which can reduce technical and commercial losses by up to 20-30%. Access must move from pilots to performance — especially for clean cooking and for deploying digital innovations that boost efficiency and productive use. 

#Digital and #AI tools can lower costs, improve planning, and support de-risking — but they are enablers, not substitutes. Community engagement, local capacity, and strong institutions remain the backbone of a just energy transition, especially where digital ecosystems are still emerging. 

Energy is ultimately about people, jobs, and dignity. This week in Dakar, with UNDP  colleagues and partners across Africa, we are working to turn the continent’s renewable wealth into universal access, green industries, and inclusive growth. 

#EnergyForDevelopment

posts.title: The 'Smart City' has been closely linked with #energy since the term was introduced. From smart energy meters, to the role of
posts.caption:
The 'Smart City' has been closely linked with #energy since the term was introduced. From smart energy meters, to the role of Big Data for energy and grid management. I've been getting more and more questions about what a 'smart' city looks like and wanted to re-share this article I co-authored with Calum Handforth  a while back. We argue that we need fewer 'smart' cities, and more 'smarter' cities. Smarter cities which:

* Put people at the heart of urban and technology planning and deployment. Not cities that try to retro-fit tech and energy projects and programmes around perceived citizen needs.
* Use a broad tech and innovation toolkit, and don’t just chase the latest innovation. For example, Big Data is important, but so too is the 'Thick Data' which helps us to learn more about energy consumers - or those that are energy-poor.
* Focus on outcomes, and not just the rollout of solutions - and, especially, we need ‘Smarter Cities’ which invest in the ‘connective tissue’ that creates meaningful urban spaces and places. We don’t want cities to just become ‘platforms’ of ‘use-cases’.

When writing this article, we were also inspired by the exciting and important opportunities for 'smart cities' in the Global North to learn from their counterparts in the Global South. 

And this is particularly relevant for energy, when so many innovations - including decentralised renewable energy, pay-as-you-go solar and other innovative business models, and frugal energy innovations - could be as relevant in New York as they are in New Delhi. 

Let me know your thoughts! https://lnkd.in/ghZnHY7g

posts.title: Digitalization and #AI are reshaping the clean energy transition, raising critical questions about skills, inclusion, and opp
posts.caption:
Digitalization and #AI are reshaping the clean energy transition, raising critical questions about skills, inclusion, and opportunity.

At the International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA)  Assembly, I joined a series of sessions exploring how digitalization and AI can strengthen integrity and efficiency, empower youth, and shape the future of renewable energy jobs. I just wanted to re-share my three reflections: 

1️⃣ Innovation in #energy is not new
While digital and AI tools are accelerating change, innovation has long driven progress in the energy sector. We have fantastic innovation talent and heritage within and across the sector - and huge opportunities to amplify this. We need to explore and embrace new tech and new opportunities, but also build on our existing learning too. 

2️⃣ A broad and future-ready talent pipeline is essential
'#Digital', 'AI', and 'energy' are not discrete or homogenous jobs or sectors. They are wide-ranging and interlinked - and even inter-disciplinary. So, when we're talking about shaping the jobs of the future, we need to think broadly. There isn't a single 'energy' job, but a whole pipeline of different opportunities and entry-points. 

3️⃣ Energy talent is everywhere
All voices need to be represented and participate in energy policy, design, and delivery. Women are still under-represented in the sector, whilst the Global South is home to phenomenal talent building and deploying energy systems and solutions. We need to empower, platform, champion, and support this next generation of energy talent - wherever it's found. 


#IRENA16A #EnergyForDevelopment

posts.title: Sustainable energy is not a nice-to-have. It is a catalyst for societies and economies, and a core driver of 21st-century ind
posts.caption:
Sustainable energy is not a nice-to-have. It is a catalyst for societies and economies, and a core driver of 21st-century industrial policy, growth, and development.

Since 2015, progress has been real. Energy transition investment reached a record USD 2.4 trillion in 2024, with renewables attracting nearly twice the funding of fossil fuels. Global electricity access rose from 87 to 92 percent between 2015 and 2023, lifting hundreds of millions out of poverty.

At the International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA)  Assembly, ahead of the 2026 High-Level Political Forum, I reflected on where #SDG7 ⚡️stands today. Three priorities stood out.

1️⃣ A just energy transition is a people’s transition.
Renewables already support more than 16 million jobs and could more than double by 2030, but skills are not keeping pace. Without urgent investment in training and stronger South-South cooperation, workforce gaps risk becoming a binding constraint on long-term development.

2️⃣ Energy security must sit at the core of SDG7.
Diversified energy systems strengthen economic resilience, protect public finances, and reduce exposure to external shocks. In many fossil-fuel-producing countries, public revenues still depend heavily on oil, gas, or coal. Clean energy transitions can reduce import dependence, improve efficiency, and strengthen economic stability rather than create new vulnerabilities.

3️⃣ Leveraging #digitalization and #AI as enablers of the transition.
From smart grids to geospatial data, digital tools improve efficiency, reduce losses from unreliable grids, and lower investment risk. As AI becomes a growing energy consumer, its benefits will depend on alignment with clean power expansion, grid investment, and clear regulatory frameworks, especially where electricity systems are already constrained.

#IRENA16A #SDG7 #EnergyForDevelopment

posts.title: For Small Island Developing States 🏝️, the energy transition is not just about reforming energy systems. It is about economic
posts.caption:
For Small Island Developing States 🏝️, the energy transition is not just about reforming energy systems. It is about economic stability, climate resilience, and national sovereignty. With renewables now cheaper than fossil fuels across most island grids, clean energy is no longer a cost—it is the smartest macro-economic choice.

Many #SIDS import the vast majority of their energy through fossil fuels. Around 60% import at least 90% of their energy, and in countries like the Maldives, fuel imports absorb more than 10% of GDP, reaching up to 16% across SIDS in some years. This dependence exposes economies to price volatility, supply disruptions, and extreme weather.

At the International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA) Assembly, I discussed how SIDS are not waiting to transition — they are already leading it. Out of necessity and innovation, they are building power systems designed for climate resilience, energy independence, and the water-energy-food nexus, from solar-powered desalination to resilient island microgrids.

The real bottleneck today is not technology — it is finance. What SIDS need are bankable investment pathways that combine concessional capital, guarantees, and risk-sharing instruments to crowd in private investors at scale. This is where digital# data and #AI become transformative: by improving demand forecasting, data transparency, grid management, and real-time performance tracking, they reduce uncertainty, lower the cost of capital, and turn small, fragmented projects into investable portfolios.

So the question is no longer whether SIDS should transition.
It is how fast we can align #finance, guarantees, and digital intelligence to unlock clean-energy investments that match their ambition — and their urgency.
#EnergyForDevelopment
#RisingUpForSIDS
#IRENA 16

posts.title: The #AI era and the energy transition are advancing rapidly –– but unequally. 565 million people in Sub-Saharan Africa still
posts.caption:
The #AI era and the energy transition are advancing rapidly –– but unequally. 565 million people in Sub-Saharan Africa still lack electricity, and 900 million rely on biomass. Whilst annual data center spending to fuel the AI boom could require investments up to USD 7 trillion by 2030.

But improving the alignment of these 21st century trends could lead to important impact. 

When planned together, digital infrastructure and AI-enabled innovation can anchor new renewable generation, create reliable offtake, and catalyze local innovation ecosystems. 

What does AI mean for development if it does not change how people access energy, cook, or economic opportunities? During a Ministerial Address at the International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA)  Assembly, I delved into what development-centered and meaningful AI-energy alignment looks like: 

1️⃣ AI is accelerating renewable deployment by turning planning into precision delivery: AI-enabled forecasting, digital twins, and grid analytics improve dispatch accuracy by 20-30% and cut curtailment by 10-12%, enabling faster integration of wind and solar at scale.

2️⃣ Digital systems are converting efficiency gains into fiscal space for access and inclusion: Energy inefficiency still drives nearly 60% of global energy losses, costing developing economies up to USD 1.3 trillion by 2030. Even a 10% efficiency gain, enabled by AI-based demand management and predictive maintenance, can unlock billions in savings.

3️⃣ Livelihood creation through productive use of energy: When energy and digital transitions converge, they create jobs, incomes, and development. And as clean energy is combined with digital tools, data, and market intelligence, it becomes a platform for economic transformation.

With this emerging technology, we have the opportunity to revolutionize our energy systems, but only if AI is deliberately aligned with access, affordability, and resilience, rather than layered onto existing inequalities.

posts.title: The energy transition will not be driven by ambition alone—it will be shaped by whether we can turn global capital into real,
posts.caption:
The energy transition will not be driven by ambition alone—it will be shaped by whether we can turn global capital into real, investable clean-energy markets where energy demand, development needs, and climate goals intersect. 

In 2024, global investment in energy transition technologies reached a record $2.4 trillion, up 20% from 2023. Yet more than 90% of these flows went to China and advanced economies, even as fossil fuel subsidies remain at $1.1 trillion and external debt servicing reached $1.4 trillion, with 61 countries spending over 10% of public revenues just to cover interest payments.

At the UNDP  session today at the @IRENA Pavilion during #WFES2026, we focused on how to do exactly that, looking at the 3 financial solutions that unlock opportunity:

1️⃣ Strengthening local ownership and value chains is essential to turn renewable deployment into development. In regions such as North Africa, capacity is scaling rapidly, but external ownership and export-oriented models limit job creation, skills, and domestic value capture.

2️⃣ Using debt-smart and blended finance instruments can restore fiscal space for clean energy. In non-oil-producing MENA countries, debt-to-GDP ratios approaching 90% are crowding out public investment in energy, health, and education—making guarantees, concessional capital, and debt-linked climate finance critical.

3️⃣ De-risking and demand-anchoring mechanisms can lower the cost of capital. Today, renewable projects in high-risk markets face financing costs two to three times higher than in advanced economies, even though the technologies are the same.

These realities point to a simple truth: scaling clean energy without reforming financial systems will reproduce inequality. The future of a just transition lies in what we learn - and change - when capital is structured to reduce risk, retain value locally, and support inclusive investment, energy solutions become affordable, resilient, and scalable—making a just energy transition the engine for development pathways that are truly sustainable.

#EnergyForDevelopment #WFES2026 #DevelopmentFinance #Derisking

posts.title: We are now in the #Zettabyte era - generating volumes of data never seen before in human history. With just one zettabyte equ
posts.caption:
We are now in the #Zettabyte era - generating volumes of data never seen before in human history. With just one zettabyte equivalent to a trillion gigabytes, we often hear data being called the the new oil, gold, or currency. But data only creates value when it is translated into decisions. 

Data centres already consume 1.5–2% of global electricity, rising to 5–20% in major digital hubs, while putting growing pressure on power systems, water, and land. 

At the same time, when the just energy transition and the digital revolution are planned together, clean power and data reinforce each other. When clean energy is combined with digital tools, data, and market intelligence, it becomes a platform for jobs, livelihoods, and sustainable development — not just electrons.

This is why, at UNDP , we are working closely with governments and energy partners to turn data into a development asset for the AI and energy transition. Earlier today, at #WFES2026 we reflected on what we are learning in practice. 
Three strategic insights stand out:

1️⃣Data, digital and AI are now a core asset for clean energy investment and delivery. High-quality energy data can de-risk projects and attract capital — but only if digital energy systems are cyber-secure. As grids become digital, cybersecurity becomes energy security, protecting hospitals, water systems, and local businesses. Geospatial and context-specific data can significantly improve energy planning, identify viable investments, and accelerate rollout.

2️⃣ Focus must shift from data systems to data ecosystems. Energy solutions increasingly generate data, but transformational impact depends on how these data flow across institutions, sectors and stakeholders. Building inclusive energy ecosystems requires systems-level approaches; linking data, energy priorities and development objectives, from national policy to local delivery.	

3️⃣ Data transparency and accountability can make energy systems inclusive. Our data shows 447 million “electrified” people do not actually use power. When energy data is transparent and well-governed, utilities and investors become accountable for who is served and who is left behind — turning energy systems into platforms for livelihoods and inclusive development, not just grid connections.

As we move deeper into the AI and energy transition, the real challenge is not generating more data - but using it effectively and governing it better, together. The future of the energy transition will be shaped not by how much data we generate, but on whether data systems reflect lived realities, enable better decisions, and align digital innovation with equitable energy outcomes

#EnergyForDevelopment #DataGovernance #WEFS #ThickData #BigData

posts.title: Green hydrogen: fuel of the future, or risking another development divide? Green hydrogen is a potential catalyst of sustaina
posts.caption:
Green hydrogen: fuel of the future, or risking another development divide?
 
Green hydrogen is a potential catalyst of sustainable development. Producing hydrogen through 100% renewable electricity could significantly reduce emissions, whilst also powering the sectors, industries, and opportunities that drive countries' growth and development. Green hydrogen could decarbonise heavy industry, support green industrialisation, create inclusive jobs, and strengthen energy security.
 
It has the potential to supply up to 12% of global energy demand by 2050.
 
But, how can we maximise its benefits - whilst avoiding creating, or entrenching, a new energy and technology divide?
 
1️⃣ Green hydrogen is not for everyone
As with other energy solutions, green hydrogen is one tool in the sustainable energy toolkit. Not every country is suited for large-scale hydrogen. Water availability, energy access needs, land use, and national development priorities must guide decisions. National leaders, and energy agencies, need to be supported and empowered to build the renewable energy portfolios that make sense for their local context.
 
2️⃣Take a holistic approach to energy planning, and don't undermine national climate priorities
Scaling hydrogen is resource-intensive, placing real pressure on land, water, and power systems. 2 million tonnes alone requires around 18 million cubic metres of water, making value creation highly sensitive to how projects are planned and governed. Hydrogen deployment needs to align with climate goals and with the responsible use of water and land. If these are in sync, the potential is considerable. .
 
3️⃣ Green hydrogen needs to deliver domestic value, and people need to come first
Jobs, skills, and local supply chains do not emerge by themselves. Domestic value capture needs to be built into project design from the outset - reaffirming the need to ensure green hydrogen is relevant to national contexts. Similarly, communities benefit only when institutions, regulation, and investment frameworks are aligned to protect resources and distribute gains fairly. Green energy needs to support people, and not just markets.
 
The potential of green hydrogen is immense. In South Africa alone, projections suggest a 3.6% increase in GDP and 370,000 new jobs by 2050. But these outcomes are not inevitable. Green hydrogen can be a powerful development accelerator. But only if it is designed intentionally to strengthen resilience, build local value, and support inclusive growth.

posts.title: Energy has been centre stage at #Davos this week. And, amid all of this: AI. AI is not artificial. It has a long tail of ener
posts.caption:
Energy has been centre stage at #Davos this week. And, amid all of this: AI. AI is not artificial. It has a long tail of energy-hungry physical data centres and GPU racks, critical mineral mining, and real-world inference demanding unprecedented power supplies.

So, how do we harness these two seemingly separate but, in reality, interconnected and intertwined revolutions - the energy transition, and the AI era? This is the focus of our new Bulletin, below, where we define the ‘digital energy stack’.

In the tech world, a ’stack’ is the collection of different technologies and components needed for a digital product or service to function. As you read this post, it sits on a ’stack’ of solutions: a web browser or LinkedIn application on your phone or other device. Internet and email protocols that (hopefully!) are displaying the below graphic and link correctly. And, layers of cloud hosting, connectivity, and - of course - energy, to make all of this happen.

We are applying this ‘stack’ approach to sustainable energy. We need a systems-level approach, and coherent and strategic efforts. There are seven elements in the ’digital energy stack’:

📊 𝐃𝐚𝐭𝐚 - the 'fuel' of the energy revolution. Big, Lean, and Thick Data.
📱 𝐂𝐨𝐧𝐧𝐞𝐜𝐭𝐢𝐯𝐢𝐭𝐲 - including 3G and 4G, and IoT.
🖥️ 𝐂𝐨𝐦𝐩𝐮𝐭𝐞 - the 'currency' of the 21st century.
🪪 𝐃𝐢𝐠𝐢𝐭𝐚𝐥 𝐏𝐮𝐛𝐥𝐢𝐜 𝐈𝐧𝐟𝐫𝐚𝐬𝐭𝐫𝐮𝐜𝐭𝐮𝐫𝐞 - to amplify the impact of inclusive energy.
🔒 𝐂𝐲𝐛𝐞𝐫𝐬𝐞𝐜𝐮𝐫𝐢𝐭𝐲 - recognising energy's status as critical national infrastructure. 
🤖 𝐀𝐈 - with AI driving new energy solutions, but also creating new challenges.
🏛️ 𝐆𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐧𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞 - shaping the talent, culture, and  institutions of the energy transition.

Importantly, there is no single pathway for any of these seven components. Digital and energy innovation is occurring and emerging everywhere, from Silicon Valley to the Silicon Savannah. The Global South is not just an innovation taker - but a maker, and shaper.

Without intentional design, digital risks reinforcing and entrenching energy inequality rather than accelerating an inclusive and just energy transition. The question is no longer whether AI and energy will intersect. It is whether we design that intersection to deliver development, resilience, and equity at scale.

posts.title: Clean Energy in the Age of Data and AI: How Data and AI Are Reshaping Clean Energy and Development? 26 January marks the Inte
posts.caption:
Clean Energy in the Age of Data and AI: How Data and AI Are Reshaping Clean Energy and Development?

26 January marks the International Day of Clean Energy, a moment to reflect on how we deliver equitable and sustainable energy transitions that leave no one behind and protect our planet.

For every generation, energy progress has never been just about technology—it has been about expanding what people and societies are able to do. Steam turned heat into motion and powered the first industrial surge. Electricity multiplied development, bringing light to homes, power to industry, and refrigeration that keeps food and vaccines safe. Today, clean energy is becoming the backbone of a new development era—one increasingly shaped not only by electrons, but by data and artificial intelligence.

AI-enabled forecasting and optimisation can unlock up to 175 GW of additional transmission capacity without building new lines, delivering power to millions of people. In practice, better forecasting has already increased wind power value by up to 20% and reduced outage duration by as much as half in some systems.

But this impact is not automatic. Without deliberate design and governance, data and AI can deepen strain on energy systems. When used intentionally, they can strengthen access, resilience, and fairness, and help deliver a just energy transition.

So how do we maximise these gains without creating or entrenching a new digital and energy divide?

1️⃣ Energy data must be treated as public infrastructure
Open, trusted data on demand, grid capacity, and system performance reduces uncertainty and unlocks investment at scale. When data is shared, the benefits of AI and digital tools can move from pilots to systems.

2️⃣ AI and energy must operate within land, water, and social limits
Efficiency gains matter only if they respect resource constraints and local realities. Digital optimisation cannot come at the expense of people or ecosystems.

3️⃣ Al needs to deliver for people
The growth of energy, digital, and AI should be judged by whether intelligence expands access, resilience, and livelihoods, not just system performance.
The opportunities are real. Data and AI can accelerate the energy transition in ways we have never seen before. 

But only if they are governed deliberately, aligned with development goals, and designed to serve people first.

#InternationalDayOfCleanEnergy #CleanEnergyDay #AI

Yet nearly two out of every five people in Africa still lack electricity, as population growth continues to outpace connections. Progress is happening — but not yet at the speed or scale required.

The opportunity is immense. Africa holds 60% of the world’s best solar resources, more than 7,900 GW of solar potential, over 400 GW of hydropower, and vast wind and geothermal corridors. These resources position Africa to build clean, resilient energy systems that power development, jobs, and economic transformation.

As energy demand grows, the challenge is no longer only expanding access — but how to use data, digitalization, and AI to plan better, invest smarter, and deliver faster. Digital intelligence can help turn clean energy into a true platform for inclusion and growth.

posts.title: Digitalisation of energy systems is not just a technical pathway. It is a development choice. It shapes energy reliability fo
posts.caption:
Digitalisation of energy systems is not just a technical pathway. It is a development choice. It shapes energy reliability for households, competitiveness for industries, and fiscal efficiency for states.

AI and advanced digital tools can already reduce technical and commercial losses by 10–30%, improve grid flexibility, and accelerate the integration of variable renewables through forecasting, demand response, and predictive maintenance. But scale changes the equation. 

As digital infrastructure expands: how do we grow an already energy-intensive digital sector in a way that is efficient, fair, and sustainable?

The stakes are real. In South Asia, low-income households spend over 10% of their income on basic energy services, while grid losses reach 17–20%. At the same time, data centres are projected to consume around 945 TWh of electricity by 2030, with significant water demands.

Three priorities help reframe the challenge:

🏭 Treat digital loads as industrial policy
Clean, flexible power systems are needed to support energy-intensive digital infrastructure without locking in new emissions.

♻️ Turn digital footprints into community benefits
Clean energy supply for AI should be guided by system-level planning, not narrow self-sufficiency approaches. When integrated into power and urban systems, digital infrastructure can anchor new renewable capacity, enable waste-heat recovery and circular energy use, and support the wider electrification of transport, industry, and surrounding communities.

🌍 Use planetary intelligence as a guiding framework
AI can help interpret and protect ecological limits, supporting digital systems that work with planetary boundaries, not against them.

Digital acceleration strengthens development only when built on renewable, reliable, and affordable energy systems. The real question is not whether AI and energy will intersect, but how we design that intersection to deliver equity and resilience at scale.

Find more in Sustainable Energy Bulletin 👉 https://bit.ly/3Zn7Wj4

posts.title: Global electricity demand is projected to grow by 3.6% annually between 2026 and 2030, driven by industry, electric mobility,
posts.caption:
Global electricity demand is projected to grow by 3.6% annually between 2026 and 2030, driven by industry, electric mobility, cooling and data centres. Emerging economies will account for nearly 80% of additional demand, placing the Global South at the centre of this transformation. At the same time, renewables are set to overtake coal, with renewables and nuclear reaching 50% of global generation by 2030, up from 42% today, while solar and wind rise from 17% to 27%. This shift creates a historic opportunity to align energy expansion with development and industrial transformation. 

Yet affordability remains a critical constraint, as electricity prices in many countries have risen faster than incomes since 2019. The pathway forward lies in designing power systems that deliver efficiency across demand, supply and infrastructure use—through smart grids, regional interconnections, demand-side management, and blended finance mechanisms that crowd in private capital while protecting vulnerable households.

Unlocking these opportunities requires three interconnected solutions:

1. Scale grids and storage at speed. Annual grid investment must increase by roughly 50% from today’s USD 400 billion, combined with accelerated deployment of utility-scale batteries to enhance flexibility and energy security.

2. Develop integrated, development-focused energy systems. Combining grid expansion, distributed renewables, storage and digital system management can support electrification of transport, industry and communities while reducing import dependence.

3. Ensure affordability and financial sustainability. Smart market design, demand-side efficiency, regional interconnections and blended finance mechanisms can crowd in private capital, protect vulnerable households and stabilize prices.

With global power sector emissions plateauing through 2030, the just energy transition is no longer a future aspiration—it is a present reality. The Global South is already demonstrating leadership in renewable expansion and system innovation, proving that development and decarbonization can advance together, and setting the pace for a more resilient and inclusive global energy system in our societies.

Selwin Hart Alexander De Croo Damilola Ogunbiyi Francesco La Camera Fatih Birol Agostino Inguscio Dr. Abdallah Dardari  Ali Saffar

posts.title: How can countries leverage green hydrogen to decarbonize hard-to-electrify industries while strengthening development outcome
posts.caption:
How can countries leverage green hydrogen to decarbonize hard-to-electrify industries while strengthening development outcomes?

Global hydrogen demand reached 100 million tonnes (Mt) in 2024, growing by nearly 2% from 2023, in line with overall energy demand growth. Yet it is still produced almost entirely from fossil fuels, consuming around 290 billion cubic metres of natural gas and 90 million tonnes of coal equivalent each year. The transition to low-emissions hydrogen is therefore not marginal — it is systemic.

For emerging and developing economies, this transition represents a strategic development opportunity.

Hard-to-electrify sectors such as steel, chemicals, refining, shipping and aviation will require energy-dense, low-carbon fuels. If designed well, green hydrogen can reduce exposure to fossil fuel volatility, strengthen energy security, create skilled jobs and anchor new industrial value chains —when guided by strong governance and development-focused strategies.

Our report identifies three priorities to ensure green hydrogen supports equitable development:

⚖️ Build strategic foundations before committing to scale
With global hydrogen demand still dominated by fossil-based supply and costs for low-emissions hydrogen remaining 2–4 times higher in many regions, countries should prioritize phased pilots. Strategic demonstration projects allow learning, cost discovery, and institutional strengthening without creating fiscal or technological lock-in.

🔗 Integrate green hydrogen into broader industrial policy
Hydrogen should not be treated as a standalone sector. It must be embedded in coordinated energy planning, renewable capacity expansion, infrastructure development, skills strategies, and industrial upgrading. Given that hydrogen production requires large volumes of additional renewable electricity, system-level planning is essential to avoid diverting clean power away from households and productive sectors.

💰 De-risk strategically with governance safeguards
Blended finance, carbon contracts for difference, and public guarantees can help close viability gaps and crowd in private capital. But de-risking must be conditional on environmental safeguards, renewable additionality, water sustainability, local job creation, and transparent revenue frameworks to ensure that hydrogen projects contribute to long-term development outcomes.

UNDP is working with countries to translate these principles into practical strategies—supporting hydrogen roadmaps, identifying bankable projects, and aligning development with jobs, skills, environmental safeguards, and local industrial priorities.

For sectors where direct electrification is not feasible, green hydrogen can provide a pathway toward net-zero when aligned with inclusive development goals.

posts.caption:
Can countries expand power systems without deepening energy poverty?

Global electricity demand is projected to grow by around 3.6% annually through 2030, driven by electrification of industry, cooling, transport, and digital services. As countries expand grids and generation capacity to meet rising demand, the scale of investment required is substantial.

Yet this expansion coincides with a persistent access and affordability gap. While around 92% of the global population had basic electricity access in 2023, 666 million people still remained without electricity, with the access gap heavily concentrated in Sub-Saharan Africa.

But this moment is not only a development challenge — it is a strategic opportunity.
The acceleration of electricity demand can unlock new models of partnership, mobilize private capital at scale, and align infrastructure expansion with inclusive growth. With the right policy signals, regulatory clarity, and risk-mitigation instruments, private sector engagement can help close the financing gap while advancing affordability and equity.
Three approaches highlighted in UNDP’s From Commitments to Megawatts bulletin stand out:

💰 Implement targeted subsidies and financial mechanisms
Affordability remains a major barrier. UNDP analysis shows that only 22% of households without electricity can afford basic solar kits without support. Targeted subsidies can significantly expand uptake. In Togo, reducing PAYGo solar costs by 18–42% led to a 122% increase in adoption, with the strongest gains in underserved communities.

🔌 Scale decentralized renewable energy
Off-grid solar and mini-grids remain among the most cost-effective pathways to reach remote populations. These solutions have already provided electricity to over 560 million people globally, with the potential to reach nearly 400 million more by 2030 at lower cost than grid extension.

📊 Leverage data-driven energy planning
Data-driven tools such as least-cost power development planning enable governments to expand grids while prioritizing areas with the largest affordability and reliability gaps—ensuring that investments strengthen both capacity and inclusion.

UNDP is working with countries to translate these approaches into practical strategies—supporting integrated energy planning, financial de-risking, tariff reform, and decentralized renewable deployment that aligns infrastructure expansion with inclusive and sustainable development.

As electricity demand accelerates, the question is not only how fast systems grow—but whether expansion ensures affordability and equity.

posts.caption:
As energy systems go more digital, they also become more exposed. The spread of IoT devices, data platforms, and AI-driven operations has widened the attack surface. Whilst deeper integration between digital and energy systems introduces new risks for resilience.
 
This is why cybersecurity needs to be designed in from the start. Digital tools and AI are increasingly central to how energy systems operate, but without the right governance, skills, and safeguards, they can also amplify vulnerabilities. Cyber incidents can disrupt power supply, compromise data, and undermine trust. With immediate social and economic consequences.
 
Countries around the world are already leaning-in. Including through:
 
🔐 Embedding cybersecurity and resilience-by-design standards across digital and energy infrastructure
📡 Strengthening incident response, reporting requirements, and accountability for critical energy systems
🧑‍💻 Building sector-specific cybersecurity skills and awareness across energy institutions, businesses, and amongst consumers

posts.title: Can countries double energy efficiency while electricity demand accelerates? With electricity demand expected to grow 3.6% an
posts.caption:
Can countries double energy efficiency while electricity demand accelerates?

With electricity demand expected to grow 3.6% annually through 2030, driven by digitalization, AI, cooling, and electrification, efficiency is one of the fastest ways to reduce energy system costs. Global efficiency-related investment is set to reach almost USD 800 billion in 2025, over 70% since 2015.

The UAE Consensus commits countries to tripling renewables and doubling efficiency improvement rates to around 4% annually by 2030. Yet gains were only 1% in 2024 and are projected to reach just 1.8% in 2025.

Efficiency is an opportunity for the Global South. It reduces exposure to volatile electricity prices and has already avoided the need for 20% more fossil fuel imports. 

Since 2000, efficiency improvements have cut household energy bills in advanced economies by up to 20%, while industries now produce 20% more value per unit of energy than in 2000. 

Three coordinated areas can accelerate energy efficiency implementation solutions:

⚡ Strengthen national efficiency frameworks
Embedding efficiency targets into digital, industrial, and affordability policies is critical to reach the required 4% annual improvement rate. Brazil’s Artificial Intelligence Plan allocates over $900 million to support sustainable energy systems for data centers and AI infrastructure, demonstrating how digital strategies can align with national efficiency and decarbonization pathways.

💻 Reduce cooling demand for datacenters and digital infrastructure intensity 
Cooling systems account for between 7% of total electricity consumption in highly efficient hyperscale data centres and over 30% in less-efficient enterprise facilities.

📊 Deploy AI for system-wide optimization
AI can map infrastructure gaps, anticipate demand, and optimize energy flows in real time. AI is estimated to contribute up to 5.4 GtCO2e in annual emissions reductions by 2035 through accelerating low-carbon transitions across sectors.

UNDP  is supporting countries in aligning digital transformation with energy efficiency—integrating governance frameworks, smart infrastructure, and system optimization with sustainable development goals.

As electricity systems expand, efficiency must scale alongside demand to prevent rising costs, system strain, and stalled development progress.

posts.title: Green hydrogen could supply up to 12% of global energy demand by 2050. Yet today, less than 1% of production is low-carbon, a
posts.caption:
Green hydrogen could supply up to 12% of global energy demand by 2050. Yet today, less than 1% of production is low-carbon, and much of the investment remains concentrated away from many of the Global South’s lowest-cost production regions.

The question is not only whether green hydrogen can scale, but whether it will strengthen national development and improve people’s lives, or primarily serve external energy demand.

For countries in Africa, Latin America, and the Middle East, green hydrogen offers real opportunities: supporting industrial development, creating jobs, strengthening energy security, and diversifying economies. Some estimates suggest that hydrogen-related value chains could generate hundreds of thousands of jobs in emerging markets if local industries and skills are developed. But without careful planning, it risks repeating extractive models where resources are exported while local value creation remains limited.

Producing 1 kg of green hydrogen can require around 9 liters of purified water, meaning that large-scale projects may demand millions of cubic meters of water in regions that are already water-stressed. Land requirements are also significant: producing 1 million tons of hydrogen can require around 30,000 hectares of solar capacity, raising important questions about land use and ecosystem protection.

This is why UNDP , together with the TIDE Centre, University of Oxford, developed the 3P framework — People, Planet, and Prosperity. The framework helps ensure that hydrogen strategies align with national development priorities, operate within ecological limits, and generate shared economic benefits.
I will be discussing these issues at the European Hydrogen Energy Conference (EHEC)  (EHEC 2026) in Seville on 12 March, during Plenary Session 3: Energy Security Profiles for the Global Transition.

Join the conversation at European Hydrogen Energy Conference (EHEC)  2026:
📆 12 March 2026
📍 Moeve Auditorium, FIBES, Seville
🕦 11:30–13:30
🎟️ Register: https://lnkd.in/d5fNFrxH

Hydrogen’s success will depend not only on scale, but on whether it delivers shared prosperity.

posts.title: Green hydrogen is often labelled the “fuel of the future,” projected to meet up to 12% of global energy demand by 2050. But c
posts.caption:
Green hydrogen is often labelled the “fuel of the future,” projected to meet up to 12% of global energy demand by 2050. But can this transition also become an opportunity the Global South?

Today at the European Hydrogen Energy Conference (EHEC) , I discussed how green hydrogen could help reduce fossil fuel dependence and strengthen energy security. Yet nearly 99% of hydrogen production still relies on fossil fuels.

The EU Industrial Accelerator Act offers an important reference for boosting local industry, jobs, and clean technologies. However, hydrogen investment remains highly concentrated: 83% of global investments are located in Europe and China, highlighting the challenges many emerging economies face in attracting investment and building domestic hydrogen industries.

Green hydrogen could be a pivotal opportunity for the Global South to decarbonize industrial sectors, but the key question is how to scale this opportunity in ways that deliver real benefits for people, the planet, and long-term economic growth.

1. Green hydrogen should strengthen human capital and energy systems.
For many countries in the Global South, hydrogen offers an opportunity to diversify economies and capture first-mover advantages in emerging clean industries. With abundant solar and wind resources, production costs could reach $1.15–$1.74/kg by 2050, compared with $2.8–$4+ in many Global North countries.

2. Expansion must operate within environmental limits.
Around 70% of planned electrolyser capacity is located in water-stressed regions. Energy security cannot come at the expense of water security and ecosystem protection.

3. Financing green hydrogen must generate inclusive growth.
Many of the world’s lowest-cost hydrogen production sites still face renewable financing costs 24–32% higher than in the Global North, limiting their ability to scale.

Diversification can strengthen energy security — but not on its own. Turning green hydrogen’s potential into real progress requires policies that translate this opportunity into local jobs, resilient energy systems, and sustainable economic development.
UNDP #greenhydrogen #energyfordevelopment 
Amir Lebdioui Alexander De Croo Marcos Neto

posts.title: Are we paying trillions to avoid investing billions? Today, 2.1 billion people, about one in four globally, still cook with p
posts.caption:
Are we paying trillions to avoid investing billions? 
  
Today, 2.1 billion people, about one in four globally, still cook with polluting fuels. In sub-Saharan Africa, only 7% of rural households have access to clean cooking. 
  
The economics are just as stark. Dirty cooking costs the global economy an estimated $2.4 to $4 trillion each year through health impacts, environmental damage, and lost productivity. Yet global investment in clean cooking remains around $2.5 billion annually, less than a third of what is needed. 
  
That is not just a funding gap. It is a priorities gap. 
  
Clean cooking is still seen only as a household issue, when in reality it sits at the intersection of health, development, gender equality, and economic productivity. 
  
It reflects a whole-of-system value chain and national ecosystem, from energy planning and fuel supply chains to financing, data systems, and last-mile delivery, that treats clean cooking as essential infrastructure, not an afterthought. 
  
Three shifts are especially important: 
  
1️⃣ Integrate clean cooking into national energy planning 
Clean cooking cannot remain siloed. Embedding it in electrification strategies, renewable energy deployment, and broader energy access planning can help solutions reach more people, faster and more sustainably. 
  
2️⃣ Design financing that reaches rural and low-income households 
Upfront costs remain the biggest barrier for the households that need clean cooking most. Grants, subsidies, and innovative financing models are essential where market forces alone will not deliver. 
  
3️⃣ Use digital tools to improve targeting and efficiency 
Demand mapping, spatial planning, remote monitoring, and results-based financing can help make clean cooking programmes more effective, affordable, and scalable. 
 
In a world building artificial intelligence, smart grids, and autonomous vehicles, we cannot afford to leave a quarter of the world’s population without access to clean cooking.  
 
The technologies exist. The solutions are known. What is needed now is sustained commitment and investment to translate solutions into real change for each of the 2.1 billion people who still lack access to clean cooking. 
  
#EnergyForDevelopment #CleanCooking #SDG7

posts.title: Can the energy transition become the largest development investment opportunity of this decade? We are entering a new phase o
posts.caption:
Can the energy transition become the largest development investment opportunity of this decade?

We are entering a new phase of the global energy transition. The question is no longer whether it is happening, but whether our systems, our finance, and our institutions are moving fast enough to keep up with development realities. 

Energy is now at the centre of economic resilience and national security, making diversification of clean energy mixes a key opportunity to strengthen resilience in the context of rising geopolitical tensions. In 2024, investment in clean energy technologies reached USD 2.4 trillion. 
Demand for critical minerals could triple by 2030. Electricity demand is expected to grow more than 50 percent faster in the next decade than in the previous one, driven by electrification, cooling, and the rapid expansion of digital infrastructure—
But development realities are moving even faster. Regions where demand is growing fastest still receive a fraction of global investment.

This is exactly why, as @UN energy  partners, we bring together policy, finance, technology, and development efforts across the UN system and beyond, to move from fragmented actions to a coordinated, system-wide response—linking energy access, clean cooking, and just transition pathways.

UN-Energy connects expertise across energy, health, food, education, industry, finance, and digital to deliver at scale, responding to this new phase of the energy transition that requires integrated, interconnected solutions.

This week, I will be in Geneva for the #SDG7 Expert Group Meeting, convened by @UN DESA and hosted by UNECE - United Nations Economic Commission for Europe . The discussions will help shape the policy conversations leading into the HLPF and identify practical ways to accelerate progress on energy access and energy transitions, including clean cooking and resilient, diversified energy systems.

Looking forward to engaging with colleagues and partners in Geneva on how we can deliver a final push toward SDG7.
#SDG7 #EnergyforDevelopment #SustainableDevelopment #UNEnergy

posts.title: We measure energy access progress in kilowatt-hours, but the real question is: kilowatt-hours for what? Energy is now at the
posts.caption:
We measure energy access progress in kilowatt-hours, but the real question is: kilowatt-hours for what?
 
Energy is now at the centre of economic resilience and national security. In recent weeks alone, oil prices have surged by up to 50 percent. At the same time, clean cooking remains the furthest behind, affecting over 2 billion people and closely linked to health, gender, and air quality outcomes.
 
As we move closer to 2030, the challenge is no longer ambition, but delivery, scale, and impact.
 
This was the focus of today’s discussions at the #SDG7 Expert Group Meeting in Geneva, where I moderated Interactive Discussion 1: “Mobilizing a Final Push Towards SDG7.” The meeting was convened by UNDESA and hosted by UNECE Sustainable Energy  in preparation for the 2026 SDG7 review at the High-Level Political Forum.
 
Three priorities stood out for the final push toward SDG7.
 
🔹 First, unlocking private sector capital at scale. Up to 90% of financing across energy systems will need to come from international private capital in most countries. The constraint is not the volume of finance, but its cost and risk. We need to move beyond funding toward financial architecture by scaling blended finance, guarantees, and risk-sharing mechanisms.
🔹 Second, strengthening policy coherence and governance for energy security and resilience. Energy poverty is increasingly concentrated in fragile and conflict-affected settings. 13 of 18 countries with the largest access deficits are affected by conflict. Progress depends not only on infrastructure, but on strong national systems, including local financial ecosystems, institutional capacity, maintenance, and skills that can enable the diversification of energy systems toward clean, affordable, and accessible energy.
🔹 Third, acting as one UN system to integrate energy into national development strategies and deliver on country priorities. 2 in 3 health facilities in low- and middle-income countries still lack reliable energy. Energy is deeply interconnected with agriculture, health, industry, and livelihoods, making it the operational backbone of the development. This creates an opportunity to advance integrated systems that align access, affordability, and productive use to deliver greater impact.
 
If we act as a system and align policy, finance, and delivery, we can turn the energy transition into the largest development opportunity of this decade.
 
This means focusing on impact: cleaner air, better health, gender equality, economic opportunity, and reaching 1.18 billion people who live in energy poverty, lacking adequate, reliable, and affordable energy for essential daily activities.
 
This is why the SDG7 review at the 2026 High-Level Political Forum will be such a critical moment for global development.
 
Looking forward to continuing these conversations and working with partners to deliver the final push toward SDG7.
 
#SDG7 #EnergyForDevelopment #SustainableDevelopment #UNEnergy

posts.title: If we already know the solutions and have the technologies, what is still preventing delivery at scale? This was the central
posts.caption:
If we already know the solutions and have the technologies, what is still preventing delivery at scale?

This was the central question on day two of the #SDG7 Expert Group Meeting and UN-Energy meetings in Geneva, gathering partners to accelerate real impact by 2030 ahead of the 2026 #HLPF.

The context is stark. We are entering a fundamentally different phase — one where the global energy system remains tied to fossil fuels, supply is concentrated, and every shock hits the most vulnerable hardest.

Consider the scale of misaligned priorities:
	∙	By 2030, data centres and AI alone could consume over 1,000 terawatt-hours annually
	∙	AI investment hit USD 1.5 trillion in 2025 and could exceed USD 2 trillion in 2026
	∙	Closing the global electricity access gap costs just USD 23 billion per year — roughly what the AI sector spends in a week
The energy transition is also increasingly about integrated value chains — from minerals to manufacturing, infrastructure, and digital systems. Lithium demand alone could increase fortyfold by 2040.

Three priorities stand out for the final push:
🔹 Integrate critical minerals into energy delivery. Clean technologies are far more resource-intensive — EVs require 6× more minerals than conventional vehicles, wind plants 9× more than gas. Supply chain resilience must be embedded in delivery models.
🔹 Position AI as a core component of the energy system. AI can improve forecasting, strengthen reliability, and reduce outages by up to 50% — making it a key enabler of a Just Energy Transition, not just a source of new demand.
🔹 Reinforce clean cooking as an urgent development priority. At current rates, 1.8 billion people will still lack access by 2030. This must be fully integrated into energy planning, financing, and delivery.

The next four years are decisive. What matters now is turning priorities into results — through stronger implementation, investable pipelines, and delivery that reaches the countries and communities furthest behind.

#SDG7 #UNEnergy #EnergyTransition #SustainableDevelopment #EnergyForDevelopment

posts.caption:

Recent geopolitical tensions have exposed just how fragile global energy systems remain—driving price spikes of up to 50% and disrupting flows that underpin nearly 20% of the global market. Yet at the same time, a new reality is emerging: demand is surging, investment is rising, and the pressure to act has never been greater.

At the @UN-Energy meeting in Geneva, the conversation shifted decisively toward solutions and what comes next. The focus was not only on the challenges—but on the opportunity windows opening within this disruption.

Because within every moment of uncertainty lies a choice: to react, or to transform.

With just a few years to 2030, the question is no longer whether we have the tools—but whether we are ready to turn opportunity into delivery, and ambition into results.

posts.title: Green industrialization is not just about scaling renewables. It is about rebuilding one of the largest energy-consuming syst
posts.caption:
Green industrialization is not just about scaling renewables. It is about rebuilding one of the largest energy-consuming systems in the global economy — where industry accounts for 30% of global energy use, yet still relies on fossil fuels for more than 60% of it.

Yesterday, I participated in the "Building from the Belém Declaration on Global Green Industrialization — First Full Meeting of Supporting Countries and Organizations", organized by UNIDO  and the Brazilian government ahead of the International Vienna Energy and Climate Forum (IVECF) . With $1 trillion in industrial decarbonization projects in the pipeline but few reaching final investment decision, three opportunities stood out:

	1.	Align energy, industry, and trade strategies. Green industrialization is becoming a source of competitive advantage. The global clean energy market could grow from $1.2 trillion to $3 trillion by 2035.

	2.	Integrate digital systems and AI into decisions. AI alone could reduce energy sector emissions by 1.3–2.6 Gt CO2 annually — equivalent to the EU's total emissions today.

	3.	Coordinate infrastructure, policy, and finance. The constraint is no longer capital. With financing costs up to 7x higher in key markets, system alignment will determine where the next generation of industry is built.

Green industrialization is now a question of system design. The countries that move first to align demand, infrastructure, and finance will not only decarbonize, they will shape the next phase of industrial growth.

#GreenIndustrialization #IVECF2026 #EnergyforDevelopment

posts.title: Energy systems are being reshaped in real time. This is not just a transition; it is reshaping the global energy economy. Yes
posts.caption:
Energy systems are being reshaped in real time. 

This is not just a transition; it is reshaping the global energy economy.

Yesterday, I had the great opportunity to participate in a session hosted by the GEIDCO(Global Energy Interconnection Development and Cooperation Organization)  at the  (International Vienna Energy and Climate Forum (IVECF) ) — where this convergence was at the centre of the discussion alongside GEIDCO's Chairman, Mr. Xin Baoan.

Rising geopolitical tensions and the rapid acceleration of AI and digital infrastructure are reshaping development priorities. Conflicts and instability are exposing the vulnerability of concentrated energy systems, reinforcing the need for resilience, security, and diversification of supply. At the same time, surging electricity demand — driven by AI and cooling needs set to triple by 2050 — is placing new and growing pressures on already strained energy systems.

Meanwhile, innovation is advancing rapidly. Clean energy technologies could reach $2 trillion by 2035, and nearly $5.8 trillion is expected to flow into grid upgrades between 2026 and 2035. Yet this opportunity remains unevenly distributed — with innovation, capital, and infrastructure still concentrated in too few countries.

Three actions are needed to change this:
	1.	Treat resilience as a core investment priority. Every $1 invested in resilient infrastructure yields more than $4 in benefits. Countries with stronger renewable systems are already better absorbing shocks. Structural investments in wind, solar, and stronger grids are the answer — not short-term subsidies that address symptoms, not system constraints.

	2.	Build the skills, institutions, and infrastructure to deliver at scale. Capacity building is not just training — it is about building the jobs and technical capability countries need to absorb rising investment, including $635 billion in digital infrastructure in 2026. With fewer than 5% of people in low-income countries holding basic digital skills, closing this gap is essential for the Global South to move from hosting digital infrastructure to building the energy systems that power it.

	3.	Strengthen South-South cooperation and regional interconnectivity. Initiatives such as the ASEAN Power Grid, Just Energy Transition Partnerships, and Mission 300 show how coordination can unlock larger, more resilient, and investable systems — and help developing countries capture more value from the transition.

This is the largest development opportunity of our time — and the moment to align systems to deliver it.
#IVECF2026 #EnergyTransition #GreenIndustrialization #SDG7

posts.title: What if the real gap in digital energy innovation is not technology, but whether national innovation systems are enabling you
posts.caption:
What if the real gap in digital energy innovation is not technology, but whether national innovation systems are enabling young builders in low-access settings?
 
That was at the heart of discussions today during the SDG 7 segment of the 2026 ECOSOC Youth Forum at the United Nations  Headquarters in New York, alongside A. Anastasia Kefalidou and Elsy T. Milan.
 
Young people are already driving solutions in energy access, mini-grid management, and digital service delivery. But to unlock many of these ideas require to create national innovation systems that connect policy, financing and technology innovation to scale.
 
This matters because over 85% of the world’s youth live in developing countries where energy poverty, climate vulnerability, and unemployment are most acute, and where innovation needs stronger support.
 
Three reflections stand out:

	1.	Scaling digital energy systems requires solutions that reflect local realities. Southeast Asia’s AI startups attracted over USD 2 billion, but in places like the Pacific, where around 1,500 languages are spoken, tools that ignore local context may scale technically while failing in practice.

	2.	Youth innovation delivers most when energy systems are built to absorb it. Young innovators are already responding to local needs. In Kenya, Nigeria, and Rwanda, youth-led pay-as-you-go solar platforms are already using IoT and mobile money data to manage connections and improve planning.

	3.	Digital energy tools matter only if they advance real development outcomes. More than 1.18 billion people still live in energy poverty, while the world enters a multi-trillion-dollar digital infrastructure investment cycle. The real question is whether capital, data, and innovation are reaching the places where they can have the greatest human impact.

Young people are not waiting to be included in the transition. They are already building it. The task now is to align systems around them so their solutions can deliver at scale.
 
#ECOSOCYouthForum #SDG7 #EnergyAccess #DigitalTransformation #YouthInnovation
